# CLI (/dev/docs/cli)

`shadcn-nsh@latest` copies registry items into an existing NSH app. The component pages use `npx shadcn-nsh@latest add <name>`; this page is the command reference.

`-c, --cwd <dir>` is the app or monorepo directory (default: the current directory). `--registry <url>` is a template containing `{name}`; `add`, `list`, `view` and `diff` use the `registry` in `nsh-ui.json` when it is omitted, or the public registry at `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/v<version>/public/r/{name}.json` — the one published with the release your CLI came from, so the files match the CLI you are running. `init` uses that public registry. Every command takes `-h, --help`; `shadcn-nsh --version` prints the version.

## init [#init]

Writes `nsh-ui.json`, installs the theme, points every `nsh.json` at it, and sets up the `@/` import alias in an app. Run it once in an app that already has `nsh.json`.

```sh
shadcn-nsh@latest init [options]
```

| Flag               | What it does                                                                                        | Default               |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `-c, --cwd <cwd>`  | App or monorepo directory.                                                                          | The current directory |
| `-y, --yes`        | Accepted for scripts; nothing prompts today.                                                        | `false`               |
| `--overwrite`      | Overwrite files that already exist.                                                                 | `false`               |
| `--theme <name>`   | Theme to install: `nsh-gallery`, `shadcn`, `solid-glass`, `apple`, `material`, `winui` or `native`. | `nsh-gallery`         |
| `--registry <url>` | Registry URL template containing `{name}`.                                                          | The public registry   |

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest init -c apps/web
```

It writes `theme.json`, `light.tokens.json`, `dark.tokens.json`, `DESIGN.md`, `lib/ui/semantics.json` and `lib/ui/theme.ts` into the app (under `packages/ui` in a monorepo), and a `tsconfig.json` when the app has none. `theme.json` and `lib/ui/semantics.json` are the theme the app is **built** with; which one they hold is recorded in `nsh-ui.json` (`"theme": "theme"`, or `"theme-shadcn"` for `--theme shadcn`), and `add` resolves a component's `theme` dependency to it, so taking a component later — `--overwrite` included — never writes the build-time theme back. `light.tokens.json` and `dark.tokens.json` are standalone DTCG 2025.10 files describing the shipped theme for design tools (Figma Variables Light/Dark modes, Tokens Studio, Style Dictionary v4), `DESIGN.md` gives coding agents the theme's tokens and design rationale, and none of these generated snapshots follow later edits to `theme.json`. `--theme shadcn` also writes `themes/shadcn/`, the same palette as a theme the app can switch to while it runs.

In an app, `init` also sets up the `@/` import alias the docs' snippets use (`@/components/ui/<name>`, `@/lib/ui/theme`): `tsconfig.json` gains `"@/*": ["./*"]` under `compilerOptions.paths` — restating the NSH mappings `.nsh/tsconfig.json` declares, because a child's `paths` replace the base's — and `nsh.json` gains `"resolve": { "alias": { "@": "./" } }` for `nsh run`/`build`/`test`, which read `nsh.json`, not tsconfig. Values it finds already there are left alone with a warning. A monorepo imports from `@workspace/ui` instead, so it is not touched.

If `nsh.json` names `tailwind.colors`, `init` ends with one line naming the theme tokens those colors shadow — a class takes the Tailwind color while `token()` and the theme take the theme's ([Override from `nsh.json`](https://shadcn-nsh.aning.dev/docs/theme#override-from-nshjson)). It is a warning: the command never fails over it, and `add` prints the same line.

## add [#add]

Copies items and their `registryDependencies` into the app, dependencies first.

```sh
shadcn-nsh@latest add [options] [components...]
```

Name at least one item, or pass `--all`.

| Flag               | What it does                                 | Default                                       |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `-c, --cwd <cwd>`  | App or monorepo directory.                   | The current directory                         |
| `-o, --overwrite`  | Replace files the app has changed.           | `false`                                       |
| `-a, --all`        | Every `registry:ui` item the registry lists. | `false`                                       |
| `--dry-run`        | Print what would be written; write nothing.  | `false`                                       |
| `--registry <url>` | Registry URL template containing `{name}`.   | `nsh-ui.json`'s registry, else the public one |

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add --all
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button --dry-run
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button --overwrite
```

A file the app lacks is written, one identical to the registry's is skipped, and one the app changed is kept unless `--overwrite`. Without `--overwrite`, `theme.json` and `lib/ui/semantics.json` gain only the keys they lack (keeping the app's own colors, style values and finishes). `theme` — named, or the dependency every component has — is the theme `nsh-ui.json` records, so in an app on `theme-shadcn`, `add theme --overwrite` writes shadcn's data back, not the default one's.

The packages the items import (`lucide`) are installed with the app's own package manager, unless its `package.json` already declares them at a version in range: an exact `"lucide": "1.66.0"` is left as written.

Naming a theme (`add theme-shadcn`) installs **one more**: `themes/shadcn/`, a theme the app can switch to while it runs (`selectTheme`), with its own `theme.json`, `semantics.json`, `light.tokens.json`, `dark.tokens.json`, `DESIGN.md` and `index.ts`. It writes nothing over the app's build-time theme, and `nsh-ui.json` stays as it is; that theme is `init --theme <name> --overwrite`.

## list [#list]

Lists the registry's items, marking the ones the app has.

```sh
shadcn-nsh@latest list [options]
```

| Flag               | What it does                               | Default                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `-c, --cwd <cwd>`  | App or monorepo directory.                 | The current directory                         |
| `--json`           | Print the catalog as JSON.                 | `false`                                       |
| `--registry <url>` | Registry URL template containing `{name}`. | `nsh-ui.json`'s registry, else the public one |

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest list
```

`✓` marks an item when any of its files is in the app; the last line counts the items and the installed ones.

## view [#view]

Prints the files `add` would write, dependencies first, at their target paths and with imports rewritten for the app. Writes nothing.

```sh
shadcn-nsh@latest view [options] <items...>
```

| Flag               | What it does                               | Default                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `-c, --cwd <cwd>`  | App or monorepo directory.                 | The current directory                         |
| `--registry <url>` | Registry URL template containing `{name}`. | `nsh-ui.json`'s registry, else the public one |

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest view button
```

## diff [#diff]

Compares the app's installed files with the registry's. Exits `1` when they differ, `2` when it could not compare.

```sh
shadcn-nsh@latest diff [options] [items...]
```

| Flag               | What it does                               | Default                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `-c, --cwd <cwd>`  | App or monorepo directory.                 | The current directory                         |
| `--registry <url>` | Registry URL template containing `{name}`. | `nsh-ui.json`'s registry, else the public one |

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest diff
npx shadcn-nsh@latest diff button
```

Without an item it lists the installed items that differ; with one it prints the changed lines. `-` is a line of the app's file that overwriting would drop, `+` one it would add. A recolored `theme.json` or customized `semantics.json` is not a difference; a missing key is.

| Exit | Meaning                                                                 |
| ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `0`  | No differences.                                                         |
| `1`  | Something differs (or there is no `nsh-ui.json`).                       |
| `2`  | The registry cannot be reached and nothing is cached: compared nothing. |

Every registry file the CLI fetches over HTTP is kept in `~/.cache/shadcn-nsh` (`$XDG_CACHE_HOME`, or `SHADCN_NSH_CACHE_DIR` when set). Offline, `diff` compares with those copies and says when they were fetched; the public registry's URL is pinned to the CLI's release, so they are that registry exactly. With no copy, it prints `diff skipped` and exits `2`, so a check can tell "could not check" from "differs":

```sh
npx shadcn-nsh@latest diff; code=$?
[ $code -eq 1 ] && echo "run shadcn-nsh@latest add <item> --overwrite"
[ $code -eq 2 ] && echo "offline — diff skipped"
```

## Hosting a registry [#hosting-a-registry]

The public registry is `registry.json` built into `public/r` and served from GitHub. To host your own, build the same files and pass its URL to `--registry`.

This repository has both steps as scripts: `bun run registry:build` and `bun run registry:serve`.

### build [#build]

Builds a registry into one JSON per item plus the `index.json` that `list` and `add --all` read.

```sh
shadcn-nsh@latest build [options] [registry]
```

The argument is the registry file (default `./registry.json`). It fails when an item's `registryDependencies` disagree with its imports.

| Flag                  | What it does       | Default               |
| --------------------- | ------------------ | --------------------- |
| `-o, --output <path>` | Output directory.  | `./public/r`          |
| `-c, --cwd <cwd>`     | Working directory. | The current directory |

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest build
```

### serve [#serve]

Serves the built registry over HTTP at `127.0.0.1` for local testing.

```sh
shadcn-nsh@latest serve [options]
```

| Flag                | What it does        | Default               |
| ------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------- |
| `-p, --port <port>` | Port.               | `4173`                |
| `-d, --dir <path>`  | Registry directory. | `./public/r`          |
| `-c, --cwd <cwd>`   | Working directory.  | The current directory |

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest serve
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button --registry "http://127.0.0.1:4173/{name}.json"
```

`serve` prints the `--registry` URL to use.

# Accordion (/dev/docs/components/accordion)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add accordion
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import {
  Accordion,
  AccordionHeader,
  AccordionItem,
  AccordionPanel,
  AccordionTrigger,
} from "@/components/ui/accordion";
```

```tsx
<Accordion>
  <AccordionItem value="a">
    <AccordionHeader>
      <AccordionTrigger first>Title</AccordionTrigger>
    </AccordionHeader>
    <AccordionPanel>…</AccordionPanel>
  </AccordionItem>
</Accordion>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build an `Accordion`:

```text
Accordion
├── AccordionItem
│   ├── AccordionHeader
│   │   └── AccordionTrigger
│   └── AccordionPanel
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Disabled row [#disabled-row]

```tsx
<AccordionItem value="gift" disabled>
  <AccordionHeader>
    <AccordionTrigger>Can I send it as a gift?</AccordionTrigger>
  </AccordionHeader>
  <AccordionPanel>Gift wrapping opens with the holiday season.</AccordionPanel>
</AccordionItem>
```

### A trigger of its own [#a-trigger-of-its-own]

The trigger takes more than one child: what you draw is laid out in the row before the chevron, in
one line, and the chevron stays at the end (it is the part that turns as the item opens).

```tsx
<AccordionTrigger>
  <Icon icon={Package} {...menuItemGlyph()} />
  <RowLabel label="Shipping" strong />
</AccordionTrigger>
```

`disabled` on the trigger takes the row's presses itself — for a row that is not an item's own (an
item's `disabled` already does that for the header's trigger).

```tsx
<AccordionTrigger disabled>Can I change my address?</AccordionTrigger>
```

### Revealed panel [#revealed-panel]

`reveal` defaults on; `start` lines the panel up past a leading icon in the trigger, and `end` keeps the same room after the content.

```tsx
<AccordionPanel reveal start={24} gap={8}>
  <Text>Within 30 days, unused and in its box.</Text>
</AccordionPanel>
```

### Controlled [#controlled]

`value` is the open items; `onChange` reports the next list.

```tsx
<Accordion value={open()} onChange={({ value }) => open.set(value)}>
  <AccordionItem value="shipping">
    <AccordionHeader>
      <AccordionTrigger first>How long does shipping take?</AccordionTrigger>
    </AccordionHeader>
    <AccordionPanel>
      Orders leave within a day and arrive in two to five working days.
    </AccordionPanel>
  </AccordionItem>
</Accordion>
```

## API [#api]

Uses `disclosureTriggerLook`, `DisclosureChevron`, and `disclosurePanel`. Every prop of [`nsh/base` Accordion](https://nsh.dev/elements/accordion) parts passes through.

| Part               | Props                                           | Description                                                 |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Accordion`        | —                                               | The stack of items.                                         |
| `AccordionHeader`  | —                                               | The heading around the trigger.                             |
| `AccordionItem`    | —                                               | One section.                                                |
| `AccordionPanel`   | `reveal` (on by default), `start`, `end`, `gap` | Revealed content, in `disclosurePanel` padding.             |
| `AccordionTrigger` | `first`, `start`, `disabled`                    | The title row, with a chevron that turns as the item opens. |

# Alert Dialog (/dev/docs/components/alert-dialog)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add alert-dialog
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import {
  AlertDialog,
  AlertDialogAction,
  AlertDialogCancel,
  AlertDialogContent,
  AlertDialogDescription,
  AlertDialogFooter,
  AlertDialogHeader,
  AlertDialogTitle,
  AlertDialogTrigger,
} from "@/components/ui/alert-dialog";
```

```tsx
<AlertDialog onAction={({ action }) => console.log(action)}>
  <AlertDialogTrigger>Delete file</AlertDialogTrigger>
  <AlertDialogContent>
    <AlertDialogHeader>
      <AlertDialogTitle>Delete file?</AlertDialogTitle>
      <AlertDialogDescription>This cannot be undone.</AlertDialogDescription>
    </AlertDialogHeader>
    <AlertDialogFooter>
      <AlertDialogCancel>Cancel</AlertDialogCancel>
      <AlertDialogAction id="delete" role="destructive">
        Delete
      </AlertDialogAction>
    </AlertDialogFooter>
  </AlertDialogContent>
</AlertDialog>
```

The box is the platform's own (`nsh/base`'s `AlertDialog.show`): UIAlertController on iOS, NSAlert
on macOS, NSH's drawing of the same box on the web, the platform dialog on Android. The parts only
fill it in — they register a title, a message and buttons, and `AlertDialogContent` shows it when
the root is open. So the box **does not follow this library's theme**, what it shows is **text
only** (no views or icons; at most one text field, `input`, where the platform's alert has one), and an Android alert takes **at most three buttons**. The
platform shows one box at a time, so a process has one: two `AlertDialog`s opened together share
it, and the second is not stacked on the first.

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build an `AlertDialog`:

```text
AlertDialog
├── AlertDialogTrigger
└── AlertDialogContent
    ├── AlertDialogHeader
    │   ├── AlertDialogTitle
    │   └── AlertDialogDescription
    └── AlertDialogFooter
        ├── AlertDialogCancel
        └── AlertDialogAction
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Against `Dialog` [#against-dialog]

`AlertDialog` asks one question and waits for the answer; `Dialog` is the app's own card.

|                            | `AlertDialog`               | `Dialog`                                  |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Who draws it               | the platform                | the app, with `dialogCard` and `backdrop` |
| What it holds              | a title, a message, buttons | any content (fields, lists, pictures)     |
| Does it follow the theme   | no                          | yes                                       |
| Escape, backdrop and swipe | off (`closeOn*` props)      | on                                        |

Use `Dialog` when the box needs content of the app's own or the app's look; use `AlertDialog` when
it is a yes/no question the system should ask.

### Roles [#roles]

`role` is what each button means, and the platform places and draws it by that: `cancel` on its
own, `destructive` in red where the platform has red.

```tsx
<AlertDialogFooter>
  <AlertDialogAction id="cancel" role="cancel">
    Cancel
  </AlertDialogAction>
  <AlertDialogAction id="delete" role="destructive">
    Delete
  </AlertDialogAction>
</AlertDialogFooter>
```

`AlertDialogCancel` is the same button with `role="cancel"`; its `id` is `"cancel"` unless named.

### The chosen action [#the-chosen-action]

`onAction` reports the `id` of the button pressed (the app's name for it, never the label), or
`null` when the box closed without one.

```tsx
<AlertDialog onAction={({ action }) => action === "delete" && remove()}>…</AlertDialog>
```

### A text field [#a-text-field]

`input` on `AlertDialogContent` adds one text field to an alert (not an action sheet) —
`defaultValue`, `placeholder`, `selectTextOnFocus`, `required` (no confirming an empty one).
`onAction` reports its text as `value` with the button chosen. Windows, Linux and the terminal
show no field there: `value` is `null`, so an app that must have the text uses a `Dialog` with
an `Input`.

```tsx
<AlertDialog onAction={({ action, value }) => action === "rename" && rename(value)}>
  <AlertDialogTrigger>Rename…</AlertDialogTrigger>
  <AlertDialogContent
    input={{ defaultValue: name(), placeholder: "Name", selectTextOnFocus: true }}
  >
    <AlertDialogHeader>
      <AlertDialogTitle>Rename the photo</AlertDialogTitle>
    </AlertDialogHeader>
    <AlertDialogFooter>
      <AlertDialogCancel>Cancel</AlertDialogCancel>
      <AlertDialogAction id="rename">Rename</AlertDialogAction>
    </AlertDialogFooter>
  </AlertDialogContent>
</AlertDialog>
```

### Awaiting the answer [#awaiting-the-answer]

An app that wants the choice before it draws anything else — `await`, then act — shows the same box
with `nsh/base`'s own `AlertDialog.show`, which resolves with `{ action, value }`. That is the app's call.
The parts above declare a box under a root of the page's, for an alert that is part of what the page
draws; the library has no imperative `show` of its own: a web alert is
always the app's own drawing, and a second way in would be two APIs for one box.

```tsx
import { AlertDialog } from "nsh/base";

const discard = async () => {
  const { action } = await AlertDialog.show({
    title: "Discard your changes?",
    description: "Your draft will be lost. This cannot be undone.",
    actions: [
      { id: "keep", label: "Keep editing", role: "cancel" },
      { id: "discard", label: "Discard", role: "destructive" },
    ],
  });
  if (action === "discard") pop();
};
```

### Action sheet [#action-sheet]

`presentation="actionSheet"` slides the box up from the bottom (a list on Android). Escape and a
press outside close it unless `closeOnEscape` / `closeOnBackdropPress` say otherwise; an alert
(`"alert"`, the default) waits for a button.

```tsx
<AlertDialogContent presentation="actionSheet">…</AlertDialogContent>
```

### Trigger [#trigger]

A string child is a `Button`; `variant` picks its look (`secondary` by default). Anything else is
drawn as given.

```tsx
<AlertDialogTrigger variant="destructive">Delete file…</AlertDialogTrigger>
```

### Controlled [#controlled]

`open` shows the box and `onOpenChange` reports every change of it — `reason` is `"triggerPress"`
when the trigger opened it, `"select"` when a button was chosen and `"cancel"` when it closed
without one.

```tsx
const open = signal(false);

<AlertDialog open={open()} onOpenChange={({ open: next }) => open.set(next)}>
  …
</AlertDialog>;
```

## API [#api]

`AlertDialog` owns the open state and the text its parts registered; `AlertDialogContent` calls
[`nsh/base` `AlertDialog.show`](https://nsh.dev/elements/alert-dialog) when it opens. The box stays
one while it is up: a part that renders again with the alert still open — a page whose layout
rebuilds its children does — stacks nothing, and the answer belongs to the app that asked.

| Part                     | Props                                                                                               | Description                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AlertDialog`            | `open`, `defaultOpen`, `onOpenChange({ open, reason })`, `onAction({ action, value })`              | The root: owns the open state and the text its parts registered.                                            |
| `AlertDialogTrigger`     | `Action`'s props — `children`, `variant`, `disabled`, and every view prop — without `onPress`       | The press that opens it; a string child is a `Button`, `variant` picking its look (`secondary` by default). |
| `AlertDialogContent`     | `presentation`, `closeOnEscape`, `closeOnBackdropPress`, `input` — the rest of `AlertDialogOptions` | The parts the box shows, and the `AlertDialog.show` call when the root opens.                               |
| `AlertDialogTitle`       | `children` (a string)                                                                               | The heading.                                                                                                |
| `AlertDialogDescription` | `children` (a string)                                                                               | The message.                                                                                                |
| `AlertDialogAction`      | `id`, `role`, `children` (a string; the `id` when left out)                                         | A choice; `role` is what it means and `onAction` reports its `id`.                                          |
| `AlertDialogCancel`      | `id` (default `"cancel"`), `children`                                                               | The same button with `role="cancel"`.                                                                       |
| `AlertDialogHeader`      | `children`                                                                                          | A group that draws nothing.                                                                                 |
| `AlertDialogFooter`      | `children`                                                                                          | A group that draws nothing; the buttons keep the order they are written in.                                 |

# Alert (/dev/docs/components/alert)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add alert
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { AlertCircle } from "lucide";

import { Alert, ALERT_ICON, AlertDescription, AlertTitle } from "@/components/ui/alert";
import { Icon } from "@/lib/ui/icons";
import { colors } from "@/lib/ui/theme";
```

The examples draw icons with `Icon` from `lib/ui/icons`; see [Icons](../icons) for adding it and picking a size and color.

```tsx
<Alert>
  <Icon icon={AlertCircle} size={ALERT_ICON} tint={colors.foreground} />
  <AlertTitle>Heads up</AlertTitle>
  <AlertDescription>You can add components to your app with the CLI.</AlertDescription>
</Alert>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build an `Alert`:

```text
Alert
├── AlertTitle
└── AlertDescription
```

## Examples [#examples]

### With an icon and a note [#with-an-icon-and-a-note]

The icon comes first, drawn at `ALERT_ICON` (16 points) in the notice's ink — the terminal draws
no icons, and there the notice is its text. The title and the note line up in the column beside
it, the note a step quieter than the title.

```tsx
<Alert>
  <Icon icon={CheckCircle2} size={ALERT_ICON} tint={colors.foreground} />
  <AlertTitle>Changes saved</AlertTitle>
  <AlertDescription>Your changes have been saved.</AlertDescription>
</Alert>
```

### A title and no note [#a-title-and-no-note]

An icon and a title are a notice of one line.

```tsx
<Alert>
  <Icon icon={CheckCircle2} size={ALERT_ICON} tint={colors.foreground} />
  <AlertTitle>A title and an icon, and no note at all.</AlertTitle>
</Alert>
```

### Destructive [#destructive]

`variant="destructive"` puts the whole notice in the danger tone: the title and the icon on it,
the note at nine tenths. The parts under the root wear it without being told — the root hands the
variant down.

```tsx
<Alert variant="destructive">
  <Icon icon={AlertCircle} size={ALERT_ICON} tint={colors.destructive} />
  <AlertTitle>Unable to process your payment.</AlertTitle>
  <AlertDescription>Please verify your billing information and try again.</AlertDescription>
</Alert>
```

### A note and no title [#a-note-and-no-title]

The note has a column and no row of its own: with no title it sits beside the icon,
and a long sentence wraps there. Put an error that needs more than one line in the note, not in
the title, which keeps to one line.

```tsx
<Alert variant="destructive">
  <Icon icon={AlertCircle} size={ALERT_ICON} tint={colors.destructive} />
  <AlertDescription>
    The connection was lost before the reply finished. Check the network and try again.
  </AlertDescription>
</Alert>
```

### A note of the app's own [#a-note-of-the-apps-own]

`AlertDescription` is a frame, not a sentence: a string is drawn in the note's type and ink, and
anything else is laid out as given — a column of lines, a link, a row of buttons. What the app puts
there carries its own ink.

```tsx
<Alert>
  <Icon icon={AlertCircle} size={ALERT_ICON} tint={colors.foreground} />
  <AlertTitle>Three checks failed</AlertTitle>
  <AlertDescription>
    <View style={{ gap: 4 }}>
      <Text style={{ color: colors.mutedForeground }}>· The card's number is not valid</Text>
      <Text style={{ color: colors.mutedForeground }}>· The card has expired</Text>
    </View>
  </AlertDescription>
</Alert>
```

### The icon's column [#the-icons-column]

A view has no selector for its children, and a child cannot be asked what it is, so the text keeps
that gutter either way: an alert without an icon starts 12 points in from its padding. Write the
icon first — it is what takes the leading column.

### How it differs from the other alerts [#how-it-differs-from-the-other-alerts]

Three things are called an alert here, and this is the quiet one:

- **this `Alert`** is a notice drawn on the page or in a form, in the app's own surface, read out by
  its `role="alert"`. It takes no presses and asks nothing: the page stays usable under it.
- **`nsh/base`'s `AlertDialog`** is the platform's own alert or action sheet
  (`AlertDialog.show(options)`): a system box over the app that asks for an answer and resolves with
  the action chosen. It looks like the operating system, not like the app.
- **this library's `alert-dialog`** is the same question in `Trigger`, `Title`, `Description`,
  `Footer` and `Action`: parts that fill in that system box, so it is the platform's — its look is
  the operating system's and its content is strings. A confirmation card the app draws itself,
  with the app's look and content of its own, is [`dialog`](./dialog).

So: a notice that can wait belongs here; a question that must be answered before anything else is
an `alert-dialog` (or `dialog`, when the box needs content of the app's own).

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through on `Alert` and
`AlertDescription`, and every prop of [`nsh` Text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text) on `AlertTitle`;
`style` goes over the look's on each. The root is `role="alert"`, so a notice is read out when it
appears.

| Part               | Props                                                         | Description                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Alert`            | `variant`: `"default" \| "destructive"` (default `"default"`) | The notice's surface: `alertLook().root()`.                                                          |
| `AlertTitle`       | —                                                             | The title, a `Text` in `alertLook().title(variant)`.                                                 |
| `AlertDescription` | —                                                             | The note: `alertLook().descriptionFrame()`, its string child `alertLook().descriptionText(variant)`. |

| Prop      | Type                         | Default   |
| --------- | ---------------------------- | --------- |
| `variant` | `"default" \| "destructive"` | `default` |

The surface is the card's, with one hairline edge and the theme's inset corners, padded 16 by 12;
the icon's column is as wide as the icon, the text's takes the rest, a gap of 12 between them.
`alertLook()` is exported for a notice the app draws itself, and `ALERT_ICON` is the size its icon
is drawn at.

# Aspect ratio (/dev/docs/components/aspect-ratio)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add aspect-ratio
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { AspectRatio } from "@/components/ui/aspect-ratio";
```

```tsx
<AspectRatio ratio={16 / 9}>
  <Image src={cover} style={{ width: "100%", height: "100%" }} />
</AspectRatio>
```

## Examples [#examples]

### A picture that keeps its shape [#a-picture-that-keeps-its-shape]

The box takes its column's width and the ratio's height; its content fills it.

```tsx
<AspectRatio ratio={16 / 9}>
  <Image src={cover} style={{ width: "100%", height: "100%" }} />
</AspectRatio>
```

### A square [#a-square]

`ratio={1}` is a square: an avatar, a swatch, a cover cut to the same width and height.

```tsx
<AspectRatio ratio={1} style={{ width: 72 }}>
  <Image src={avatar} style={{ width: "100%", height: "100%" }} />
</AspectRatio>
```

### A ratio written as CSS does [#a-ratio-written-as-css-does]

A number (`16 / 9`) or CSS's own ratio (`"16 / 9"`) say the same; `"auto"` lets the height follow
the content instead.

```tsx
<AspectRatio ratio="4 / 3">…</AspectRatio>
```

### A color block [#a-color-block]

The content is anything: a chart, a placeholder, a block's fill with its label centered. A `style`
of your own goes over the look's, so the fill and the corners are the caller's.

```tsx
<AspectRatio
  ratio={16 / 9}
  style={{ backgroundColor: token("muted"), borderRadius: shape.control }}
>
  <Text style={{ color: colors.mutedForeground }}>Weekly review</Text>
</AspectRatio>
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through (`style`, `accessibilityLabel`, `onPress`, …); `style` goes over the look's, so a caller's own width, corners or fill replace the look's and the box keeps its ratio inside them.

| Part          | Props                                                                                               | Description                                                |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AspectRatio` | `ratio`: `number`, a ratio string (`"16 / 9"`) or `"auto"` (default `1`); `children`: `JSX.Element` | A box as wide as its column and as tall as its ratio says. |

The box is as wide as its column (`width: "100%"`) and its height is that width over the ratio; its
content is clipped to it (`overflow: "hidden"`), so a picture fills the box rather than spilling out
of it. `aspectRatioLook(ratio)` is exported for a box an app draws itself.

# Attachment (/dev/docs/components/attachment)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add attachment
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { FileText } from "lucide";

import {
  Attachment,
  AttachmentContent,
  AttachmentDescription,
  attachmentGlyph,
  AttachmentMedia,
  AttachmentTitle,
} from "@/components/ui/attachment";
import { Icon } from "@/lib/ui/icons";
import { colors } from "@/lib/ui/theme";
```

The examples draw icons with `Icon` from `lib/ui/icons`; see [Icons](../icons) for adding it and picking a size and color.

```tsx
<Attachment state="done">
  <AttachmentMedia>
    <Icon
      icon={FileText}
      size={attachmentGlyph("default", "horizontal")}
      tint={colors.mutedForeground}
    />
  </AttachmentMedia>
  <AttachmentContent>
    <AttachmentTitle>build.log</AttachmentTitle>
    <AttachmentDescription>124 KB · 2 min ago</AttachmentDescription>
  </AttachmentContent>
</Attachment>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build an `Attachment`:

```text
Attachment
├── AttachmentMedia
├── AttachmentContent
│   ├── AttachmentTitle
│   └── AttachmentDescription
├── AttachmentActions
│   └── AttachmentAction
└── AttachmentTrigger
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Size [#size]

`size` is `default` (40-point media, the body's type), `sm` (32, the note's) or `xs` (28, the
note's, in a chip's corners).

```tsx
<Attachment size="sm">
  <AttachmentMedia>
    <Icon
      icon={FileText}
      size={attachmentGlyph("sm", "horizontal")}
      tint={colors.mutedForeground}
    />
  </AttachmentMedia>
  <AttachmentContent>
    <AttachmentTitle>changelog.md</AttachmentTitle>
    <AttachmentDescription>8 KB</AttachmentDescription>
  </AttachmentContent>
</Attachment>
```

### States [#states]

`state` says how the attachment is doing: `idle` (not sent yet, its edge dashed), `uploading`,
`processing`, `done`, and `error` (the danger tone through the frame, the media and the
description). Put a `Spinner` in the media while it travels.

```tsx
<Attachment state="uploading">
  <AttachmentMedia>
    <Spinner size="default" tint={colors.mutedForeground} />
  </AttachmentMedia>
  <AttachmentContent>
    <AttachmentTitle>registry.zip</AttachmentTitle>
    <AttachmentDescription>Uploading · 42%</AttachmentDescription>
  </AttachmentContent>
</Attachment>
```

### Pictures [#pictures]

`orientation="vertical"` puts the media above the text, 120 points wide, for a strip of pictures.
`AttachmentMedia` takes a picture drawn inside it: give it `variant="image"` and it fades the media
until the attachment is done or idle.

```tsx
<Attachment orientation="vertical">
  <AttachmentMedia variant="image">
    <Image src={shot} style={{ width: "100%", height: "100%" }} />
  </AttachmentMedia>
  <AttachmentContent>
    <AttachmentTitle>dark mode.png</AttachmentTitle>
    <AttachmentDescription>PNG · 840 KB</AttachmentDescription>
  </AttachmentContent>
</Attachment>
```

### Actions [#actions]

`AttachmentActions` holds what can be done to the file — a remove, a retry — beside the text, or
in the corner of a vertical attachment. `AttachmentAction` is this library's `Button`, ghost and
small, for a labeled action such as Retry. Remove is an `IconButton` in that row; there is no `onRemove`. Give the icon button a square `style` (`width` and
`height` 28) so it sits in the chip; the ghost button's own padding reads as a separate pill.

```tsx
<AttachmentActions>
  <AttachmentAction accessibilityLabel="Retry" onPress={retry}>
    Retry
  </AttachmentAction>
  <IconButton variant="ghost" size="sm" accessibilityLabel="Remove" onPress={remove}>
    <Icon icon={X} {...iconButtonGlyph({ variant: "ghost", size: "sm" })} />
  </IconButton>
</AttachmentActions>
```

### A frame that opens [#a-frame-that-opens]

`AttachmentTrigger` is a pressable over the whole frame, above the media and below the actions:
pressing the file opens it, and under the pointer it shows its own wash. Name it for screen readers.

```tsx
<Attachment>
  <AttachmentMedia>…</AttachmentMedia>
  <AttachmentContent>…</AttachmentContent>
  <AttachmentTrigger accessibilityLabel="Open README.md" onPress={open} />
</Attachment>
```

### Group [#group]

`AttachmentGroup` is a row of attachments 12 points apart that scrolls sideways when they do not
fit — the files under a message, the pictures in a composer. The row takes the platform's own feel:
no snapping, and no scrollbar.

```tsx
<AttachmentGroup>
  <Attachment>…</Attachment>
  <Attachment>…</Attachment>
</AttachmentGroup>
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through on every part;
`AttachmentAction` takes this library's [`Button`](https://nsh.dev/elements/button) props,
`AttachmentTrigger` the view's (`onPress`, `accessibilityLabel`, `disabled`, …), and
`AttachmentTitle`/`AttachmentDescription` the text's. A title or a description is one line,
truncated.

| Part                    | Props                          | Description                                                                                            |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Attachment`            | `state`, `size`, `orientation` | The frame that carries one file: `attachmentLook().root(state, size, orientation)`.                    |
| `AttachmentGroup`       | —                              | A row 12 points apart that scrolls sideways when the files do not fit: `.group`, `.groupContent`.      |
| `AttachmentMedia`       | `variant`                      | The file's icon or picture: `attachmentLook().media(size, orientation, variant, state)`.               |
| `AttachmentContent`     | —                              | The text beside the media: `attachmentLook().content(orientation)`.                                    |
| `AttachmentTitle`       | —                              | The file's name, one line, truncated: `attachmentLook().title(size)`.                                  |
| `AttachmentDescription` | —                              | How the file is doing, one line: `attachmentLook().description(state)`.                                |
| `AttachmentActions`     | —                              | What can be done to it: `attachmentLook().actions(orientation)`.                                       |
| `AttachmentTrigger`     | —                              | A pressable over the whole frame: press it to open the file.                                           |
| `AttachmentAction`      | —                              | An action on the file, this library's `Button` ghost and small: `buttonLook("ghost", { size: "sm" })`. |

| Prop          | On                | Type                                                         | Default      |
| ------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------ |
| `state`       | `Attachment`      | `"idle" \| "uploading" \| "processing" \| "error" \| "done"` | `done`       |
| `size`        | `Attachment`      | `"default" \| "sm" \| "xs"`                                  | `default`    |
| `orientation` | `Attachment`      | `"horizontal" \| "vertical"`                                 | `horizontal` |
| `variant`     | `AttachmentMedia` | `"icon" \| "image"`                                          | `icon`       |

The frame is as wide as what it holds (`default` 160 points wide at least, 120 when vertical), in
the card's fill with a hairline edge and the card's corners (`inset`'s at `xs`), 10 / 8 / 6 points
in from its edge and 8 / 6 / 4 above and below; the title is medium in the page's ink and the
description the note's size in the muted ink. The frame always pads as if it holds text, so a
media on its own sits in that padding. `attachmentLook()` and
`attachmentGlyph(size, orientation)` are exported for a frame an app draws itself.

# Avatar (/dev/docs/components/avatar)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add avatar
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Avatar, AvatarBadge, AvatarGroup, AvatarGroupCount } from "@/components/ui/avatar";
```

```tsx
<Avatar name="Ada Lovelace" style={{ width: 36, height: 36 }} />
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build an `Avatar`:

```text
Avatar
└── AvatarBadge

AvatarGroup
├── Avatar
└── AvatarGroupCount
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Initials [#initials]

`name` picks a stable hue via `avatarIdentity`.

```tsx
<Avatar name="Alan Turing" style={{ width: 40, height: 40 }} />
```

### Picture [#picture]

`src` is the picture; `name`'s initials cover it while it loads, and stay if it never arrives.

```tsx
const portraits = { ada: "https://example.com/ada.png" };

<Avatar name="Ada Lovelace" src={portraits.ada} style={{ width: 40, height: 40 }} />;
```

### Broken image [#broken-image]

A picture that fails to load leaves the initials on the ring, as a gone picture should.

```tsx
<Avatar name="Ada Lovelace" src="/missing.png" />
```

### Group [#group]

`AvatarGroup` shows the first `limit` and overlaps them (`-space-x-2`). `AvatarGroupCount` is the overflow circle's text. Size each `Avatar` the same, and size the overflow with `overflowStyle`.

```tsx
<AvatarGroup
  limit={3}
  overflowAccessibilityLabel="5 more people"
  overflow={<AvatarGroupCount>+5</AvatarGroupCount>}
>
  <Avatar name="Ada Lovelace" style={{ width: 36, height: 36 }} />
  <Avatar name="Grace Hopper" style={{ width: 36, height: 36 }} />
</AvatarGroup>
```

### Presence [#presence]

`AvatarBadge` sits on the avatar's end-bottom corner. Pass its color; say the presence in `accessibilityLabel`. The avatar does not clip it.

```tsx
<Avatar
  name="Ada Lovelace"
  accessibilityLabel="Ada Lovelace, online"
  style={{ width: 36, height: 36 }}
>
  <AvatarBadge style={{ backgroundColor: colors.up }} />
</Avatar>
```

## API [#api]

Uses `avatarIdentity` and `avatarHue`. Every prop of [`nsh/base` Avatar](https://nsh.dev/elements/avatar) passes through on `Avatar`, and every prop of [`nsh/base` AvatarGroup](https://nsh.dev/elements/avatar) on `AvatarGroup` (`limit`, `total`, `overflow`, `overflowAccessibilityLabel`).

| Part               | Props                        | Description                                                                |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Avatar`           | `name`, `src`                | A round picture or name-colored initials on the identity ring.             |
| `AvatarGroup`      | `limit`, `total`, `overflow` | The first few avatars, overlapped; the rest are `overflow`.                |
| `AvatarGroupCount` | —                            | The overflow's count, tabular and muted.                                   |
| `AvatarBadge`      | —                            | A presence circle at the end-bottom corner, ringed in the page background. |

# Badge (/dev/docs/components/badge)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add badge
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Badge } from "@/components/ui/badge";
```

```tsx
<Badge tone="accent">Beta</Badge>
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Tone [#tone]

`tone` is the theme's `Tone`; a function is read where the badge is drawn, so a value the app changes follows.

```tsx
<Badge tone="neutral">Neutral</Badge>
<Badge tone="accent">Accent</Badge>
<Badge tone="info">Info</Badge>
<Badge tone="warn">Warn</Badge>
<Badge tone="destructive">Danger</Badge>
<Badge tone="up">Up</Badge>
<Badge tone="down">Down</Badge>
```

### Variant [#variant]

`default` fills the capsule with the tone's tint; `outline` draws its edge in the tone's color instead.

```tsx
<Badge variant="outline">Draft</Badge>
<Badge tone="destructive" variant="outline">
  Failed
</Badge>
```

### Size [#size]

`default` is 20 points tall; `sm` is 18, for a chip beside a smaller row — a tool card's 32 pt tile, a list's second line. The label's size and the padding follow the height.

```tsx
<Badge size="sm" tone="info">
  Running
</Badge>
<Badge tone="info">Running</Badge>
```

## API [#api]

Gallery atom: no `nsh/base` counterpart. The children are the label, and the axes take the vocabulary of [`api-unify.md`](https://github.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/blob/main/docs/specs/api-unify.md).

| Part    | Props                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Description                                                  |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Badge` | `children` (a string, required); `tone`: `Tone \| (() => Tone)` (default `"neutral"`); `variant`: `BadgeVariant` (default `"default"`); `size`: `BadgeSize` (default `"default"`); every `nsh` view prop | A small capsule label in a neutral, toned, or outline style. |

The view props (`style`, `class`, `testID`, `role`, the accessibility ones) are spread on the capsule after the badge's own, so an app can name it to a screen reader or take it out of the layout without a wrapper.

`BadgeVariant` is `"default" | "outline"`: the two the capsule's look has. `BadgeSize` is `"sm" | "default"`, and `badgeSizes` is the table: `height`, `font` and `pad`, by size.

# Breadcrumb (/dev/docs/components/breadcrumb)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add breadcrumb
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import {
  Breadcrumb,
  BreadcrumbItem,
  BreadcrumbLink,
  BreadcrumbList,
  BreadcrumbPage,
  BreadcrumbSeparator,
} from "@/components/ui/breadcrumb";
```

```tsx
<Breadcrumb>
  <BreadcrumbList>
    <BreadcrumbItem>
      <BreadcrumbLink onPress={() => navigate("/")}>Home</BreadcrumbLink>
      <BreadcrumbSeparator />
    </BreadcrumbItem>
    <BreadcrumbItem>
      <BreadcrumbPage>Settings</BreadcrumbPage>
    </BreadcrumbItem>
  </BreadcrumbList>
</Breadcrumb>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Breadcrumb`:

```text
Breadcrumb
└── BreadcrumbList
    ├── BreadcrumbItem
    │   ├── BreadcrumbLink
    │   └── BreadcrumbPage
    ├── BreadcrumbSeparator
    └── BreadcrumbEllipsis
```

## Examples [#examples]

### A trail [#a-trail]

The steps are a row that wraps when the window is narrow; the page the trail ends at is
`BreadcrumbPage`, in the page's text color, and is announced as the current page.

```tsx
<Breadcrumb>
  <BreadcrumbList>
    <BreadcrumbItem>
      <BreadcrumbLink onPress={() => navigate("/")}>Home</BreadcrumbLink>
      <BreadcrumbSeparator />
    </BreadcrumbItem>
    <BreadcrumbItem>
      <BreadcrumbLink onPress={() => navigate("/components")}>Components</BreadcrumbLink>
      <BreadcrumbSeparator />
    </BreadcrumbItem>
    <BreadcrumbItem>
      <BreadcrumbPage>Breadcrumb</BreadcrumbPage>
    </BreadcrumbItem>
  </BreadcrumbList>
</Breadcrumb>
```

### Steps left out [#steps-left-out]

`BreadcrumbEllipsis` stands for the steps a long trail leaves out. It is named `"More"`, so a
screen reader says the trail skipped some rather than jumping from one name to the next; give it
`onPress` and `role="button"` when it opens a menu.

```tsx
<BreadcrumbItem>
  <BreadcrumbEllipsis onPress={() => openMenu()} role="button" />
  <BreadcrumbSeparator />
</BreadcrumbItem>
```

### A separator of your own [#a-separator-of-your-own]

A separator is a chevron; its children replace it (a slash, a dot, a small icon).

```tsx
<BreadcrumbSeparator>
  <Text style={{ color: colors.mutedForeground }}>/</Text>
</BreadcrumbSeparator>
```

### A step with a destination [#a-step-with-a-destination]

A step is [`nsh/base`'s Link](https://nsh.dev/elements/link), so `href` and `openWith` work as they
do everywhere else: `"system"` opens the URL outside the app, `"app"` hands it to `onOpen`.

```tsx
<BreadcrumbLink href="/components" openWith="app" onOpen={({ href }) => navigate(href)}>
  Components
</BreadcrumbLink>
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through on `Breadcrumb`,
`BreadcrumbList`, `BreadcrumbItem`, `BreadcrumbSeparator` and `BreadcrumbEllipsis`, and every prop
of [`nsh` Text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text) on `BreadcrumbPage`; `BreadcrumbLink` is
[`nsh/base`'s Link](https://nsh.dev/elements/link) with all its props (`href`, `openWith`, `onOpen`,
`onPress`, `disabled`, `hitSlop`, …). Style props go over the look's.

The trail is a `navigation` landmark named `"Breadcrumb"`; the rows under it carry no role. `nsh`
has no `listitem` role, so `BreadcrumbList` is not a `list` either: a list whose children are not
its items reads worse than a plain row, and `ItemGroup` makes the same call.

| Part                  | Props                                  | Description                                                                                                   |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Breadcrumb`          | `accessibilityLabel`                   | The trail from where the app starts to the page it shows: `breadcrumbLook().root`.                            |
| `BreadcrumbList`      | every `nsh` view prop                  | The steps as a row that wraps when the window is narrow: `breadcrumbLook().list`.                             |
| `BreadcrumbItem`      | —                                      | One step: `breadcrumbLook().item`.                                                                            |
| `BreadcrumbLink`      | `children`, every `nsh/base` Link prop | A step with a destination: `breadcrumbLook().link`, `.linkClass`.                                             |
| `BreadcrumbPage`      | —                                      | The step the trail ends at, in the page's text color and current for screen readers: `breadcrumbLook().page`. |
| `BreadcrumbSeparator` | `children`                             | The mark between steps, a chevron unless given children: `breadcrumbLook().separator`.                        |
| `BreadcrumbEllipsis`  | `accessibilityLabel`                   | The steps a long trail leaves out, named `"More"`: `breadcrumbLook().ellipsis`.                               |

| Prop                 | On                    | Type                    | Default        |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------- |
| `accessibilityLabel` | `Breadcrumb`          | `string`                | `"Breadcrumb"` |
| `children`           | `BreadcrumbLink`      | `string \| JSX.Element` |                |
| `children`           | `BreadcrumbSeparator` | `JSX.Element`           | a chevron      |
| `accessibilityLabel` | `BreadcrumbEllipsis`  | `string`                | `"More"`       |

The trail is small type in the muted ink, 6 points between steps (10 on a touch screen); a step's
link takes the text color while the pointer rests on it and the theme's focus ring with the keyboard
on it. `BreadcrumbPage` sets `accessibilityState.current` to `"page"`; pass your own
`accessibilityState` to say something else. The separator is hidden from screen readers. In a
terminal, which draws no icons, the separator is `›` and the ellipsis `…`. `breadcrumbLook()` is
exported for a trail an app draws itself.

# Bubble (/dev/docs/components/bubble)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add bubble
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import {
  Bubble,
  BubbleContent,
  BubbleGroup,
  BubbleReactions,
  BubbleText,
} from "@/components/ui/bubble";
```

```tsx
<Bubble variant="muted">
  <BubbleContent>I checked the registry output and removed the stale route.</BubbleContent>
  <BubbleReactions accessibilityLabel="Reaction: thumbs up">👍</BubbleReactions>
</Bubble>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Bubble`:

```text
Bubble
├── BubbleContent
│   └── BubbleText
└── BubbleReactions

BubbleGroup
├── Bubble
└── Bubble
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Fills [#fills]

`variant` changes the frame. `default` is the accent's fill and ink — what you send; `secondary`
the raised neutral; `muted` a quieter fill; `tinted` the accent as a soft wash; `outline` a
hairline around the page's fill; `ghost` no frame at all, for assistant text that takes the whole
width; `destructive` for a turn that failed. Every fill keeps a 1-point edge, transparent where it
has no color, so the box is the same size.

```tsx
<Bubble variant="tinted" align="end">
  <BubbleContent>Tinted: the accent as a soft wash.</BubbleContent>
</Bubble>
```

### Alignment [#alignment]

`align="end"` puts the bubble on the side of what you sent; `align="start"` (the default) on the
side of what came in. A bubble is as wide as what it holds, up to 80% of its column; a `ghost` one
uses the whole width.

```tsx
<Bubble align="end">
  <BubbleContent>Sure. Hit me with your best demo.</BubbleContent>
</Bubble>
```

### Group [#group]

`BubbleGroup` stacks consecutive bubbles from one sender 8 points apart. Each `Bubble` keeps its
own `align`.

```tsx
<BubbleGroup>
  <Bubble variant="muted">
    <BubbleContent>Hey! Want to see chat bubbles?</BubbleContent>
  </Bubble>
  <Bubble variant="muted">
    <BubbleContent>I can group messages too.</BubbleContent>
  </Bubble>
</BubbleGroup>
```

### Rich content [#rich-content]

`BubbleText` is a `Text` in the bubble's type and the ink of the variant around it. NSH has no text
inheritance — the web gives a bubble's ink to whatever its content holds, NSH does not — so content
that is not a single string (a list of paragraphs, markdown rendered into text) wears `BubbleText`
rather than knowing the variant itself. `BubbleContent` draws a string child the same way.

```tsx
<Bubble variant="default" align="end">
  <BubbleContent>
    <View style={{ gap: 6 }}>
      <BubbleText>Here is a reply in more than one paragraph.</BubbleText>
      <BubbleText>Each paragraph wears the variant's ink.</BubbleText>
    </View>
  </BubbleContent>
</Bubble>
```

### Reactions [#reactions]

`BubbleReactions` is a pill in the muted fill that hangs three quarters of its height off the
bubble's `side` edge (`bottom` by default, or `top`), 12 points in from its `align` end. The
bubble keeps the room the row hangs out on that side, so the next bubble never covers it. Name the
row for screen readers: NSH reads each glyph without context otherwise.

```tsx
<Bubble variant="muted" align="end">
  <BubbleContent>I don't need tests, I know my code works.</BubbleContent>
  <BubbleReactions
    side="top"
    align="start"
    role="image"
    accessibilityLabel="Reactions: thumbs up, surprised"
  >
    👍 😮
  </BubbleReactions>
</Bubble>
```

### A tail [#a-tail]

The sender's bottom corner is squarer than the rest. It is a recipe, not a prop — a `style` on
`BubbleContent` that reads the theme's `shape`. Use the logical corner (`borderBottomEndRadius` for
what you send, `borderBottomStartRadius` for what came in) so it follows the reading direction.

```tsx
import { shape } from "@shadcn-nsh/theme";

<Bubble variant="default" align="end">
  <BubbleContent style={{ borderBottomEndRadius: shape.control / 2 }}>On my way.</BubbleContent>
</Bubble>;
```

### A turn that acts [#a-turn-that-acts]

Give `BubbleContent` `onPress` for a quick reply or a suggestion: the pointer over it is a hand.
The frame itself takes the press.

```tsx
<Bubble variant="muted" align="end">
  <BubbleContent onPress={() => reply("I forgot my password")}>I forgot my password</BubbleContent>
</Bubble>
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through on `BubbleGroup`,
`Bubble` and `BubbleContent`; `BubbleText` takes every prop of
[`nsh` Text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text), and `BubbleContent` draws a string child as a
`BubbleText`. Style props go over the look's.

| Part              | Props              | Description                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `BubbleGroup`     | —                  | Consecutive bubbles from one sender, 8 points apart: `bubbleLook().group`.                                                            |
| `Bubble`          | `variant`, `align` | One turn's frame, as wide as what it holds up to 80% of its column: `.root(variant, align)`.                                          |
| `BubbleContent`   | `children`         | The frame and the turn, a string drawn as `BubbleText`: `bubbleLook().content(variant)`.                                              |
| `BubbleText`      | —                  | A paragraph in the turn's type and the variant's ink: `bubbleLook().text(variant)`.                                                   |
| `BubbleReactions` | `side`, `align`    | The pill hung three quarters of its height off the bubble's edge: `.reactions(side, align)`; the bubble keeps `.reactionsRoom(side)`. |

| Prop       | On                | Type                                                                                       | Default   |
| ---------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------- |
| `variant`  | `Bubble`          | `"default" \| "secondary" \| "muted" \| "tinted" \| "outline" \| "ghost" \| "destructive"` | `default` |
| `align`    | `Bubble`          | `"start" \| "end"`                                                                         | `start`   |
| `side`     | `BubbleReactions` | `"top" \| "bottom"`                                                                        | `bottom`  |
| `align`    | `BubbleReactions` | `"start" \| "end"`                                                                         | `end`     |
| `children` | `BubbleContent`   | `string \| JSX.Element`                                                                    |           |
| `children` | `BubbleText`      | `JSX.Element`                                                                              |           |

The frame is `shape.container` (12 points) with 12 points of room either side and 8 above and below;
the turn's type is the body's size (13 points with a pointer, 15 on a touch screen) with a step of
leading, in the ink the fill carries — `primary-foreground` on `default`, the page's text color on
the neutral fills, `destructive` on `destructive`. Reactions are 6 points either side, 3 above and
below, 4 apart, ringed 3 points in the card's color. `bubbleLook()` is exported for a frame an app
draws itself.

# Button group (/dev/docs/components/button-group)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button-group
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { ButtonGroup, buttonGroupLook } from "@/components/ui/button-group";
```

```tsx
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "first")}>
    Back
  </Button>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "middle")}>
    Archive
  </Button>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "last")}>
    Next
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `ButtonGroup`:

```text
ButtonGroup
├── ButtonGroupText
└── ButtonGroupSeparator
```

## Examples [#examples]

### The join [#the-join]

A view styles itself and not its children, so each button wears its own place in the group:
`item(orientation, position)` squares the sides that touch and keeps one edge per join (the one
before it), the outer sides keeping the corners and the edge the button came with. `first` at the
leading edge, `last` at the trailing one, `middle` between two others. Pair `variant="outline"`
buttons when joining bordered actions directly.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "first")}>
    Back
  </Button>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "last")}>
    Next
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

The group is `role="group"`, so a reader hears the buttons as one set.

### A column [#a-column]

`orientation="vertical"` stacks them: the top and bottom corners are clamped to `shape.container`
so capsule buttons stay tidy in a column, the touching sides are squared, and one hairline is left
between adjacent items. Shadows are dropped inside the stack so seams stay clean.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup orientation="vertical">
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("vertical", "first")}>
    Copy the path
  </Button>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("vertical", "middle")}>
    Open in a new window
  </Button>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("vertical", "last")}>
    Reveal in the file manager
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

### With a separator [#with-a-separator]

`ButtonGroupSeparator` puts a hairline between borderless filled buttons (`secondary` or
`default`). The separator turns with the group — vertical down a row, horizontal across a column —
and is hidden from screen readers.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="secondary" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "first")}>
    Cut
  </Button>
  <ButtonGroupSeparator />
  <Button variant="secondary" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "last")}>
    Copy
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

### With a text addon [#with-a-text-addon]

`ButtonGroupText` sits on the muted fill with the same outline edge (`button.outline.edge`) and
height (`controlHeight.md`) as an outline button, so it joins directly with `item(...)` and shares
one clean border.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup>
  <ButtonGroupText style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "first")}>Path</ButtonGroupText>
  <Button variant="outline" style={buttonGroupLook().item("horizontal", "last")}>
    Copy
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through on all three parts;
`style` goes over the look's on each.

| Part                   | Props                                                                | Description                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `ButtonGroup`          | `orientation`: `"horizontal" \| "vertical"` (default `"horizontal"`) | Buttons joined into one control, in a row or a column: `buttonGroupLook().root(orientation)`.                |
| `ButtonGroupText`      | —                                                                    | A word inside the group on the muted fill, joined as a button would be joined: `.textFrame()` and `.text()`. |
| `ButtonGroupSeparator` | —                                                                    | The separator's own hairline (`.separator()`), turned to the group's orientation; hidden from a reader.      |

| Prop          | Type                         | Default      |
| ------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------ |
| `orientation` | `"horizontal" \| "vertical"` | `horizontal` |

`buttonGroupLook()` is exported for a group the app lays out itself: `root(orientation)` the group,
`item(orientation, position)` the join each button wears, `textFrame()` and `text()` the word's box
and its type, and `separator()` the divider's hairline.

# Button (/dev/docs/components/button)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Icon } from "@/lib/ui/icons";
```

The examples draw icons with `Icon` from `lib/ui/icons`; see [Icons](../icons) for adding it and picking a size and color.

```tsx
<Button onPress={save}>Save</Button>
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Variant [#variant]

```tsx
<Button variant="default">Save</Button>
<Button variant="secondary">Cancel</Button>
<Button variant="outline">Outline</Button>
<Button variant="ghost">Skip</Button>
<Button variant="destructive">Delete</Button>
```

### Size [#size]

```tsx
<Button size="sm">Small</Button>
<Button size="default">Default</Button>
<Button size="lg">Large</Button>
```

A size is compact with a pointer (24 / 28 / 34 points) and roomier on a touch screen (36 / 40 / 48), where a hit slop makes the target 44 points. `sm`, `default` and `lg` are the only values: a pixel size is a geometry prop (`width`, `side`), not a scale.

### Disabled [#disabled]

```tsx
<Button disabled>Save</Button>
```

### Selected [#selected]

```tsx
<Button variant="secondary" selected={open()} onPress={toggle}>
  Filters
</Button>
```

### With an icon [#with-an-icon]

`icon` takes a lucide node and draws it before the label, sized and tinted by the variant, the size and the state (a disabled filled button's icon dims with its label). The terminal draws no icons, so there it is the label alone.

```tsx
import { Plus } from "lucide";

<Button variant="secondary" icon={Plus} onPress={add}>
  New file
</Button>;
```

### Busy [#busy]

A spinner in the icon's place (before the label when there is no icon), and no second press. A new icon, or the spinner, grows in on `motion.control`; with reduced motion it switches at once. The width follows the label at once: a layout animation would move every frame of the update, app-wide.

```tsx
<Button icon={Save} busy={saving()} onPress={save}>
  {saving() ? "Saving…" : "Save"}
</Button>
```

### Any content [#any-content]

A string is the label, and a child that changes (`{count()}` beside other children) is followed the same way. Anything else is drawn as given; `buttonLabel` and `buttonGlyph` give it the button's type and icon size.

```tsx
<Button variant="secondary">
  <Badge>3</Badge>
  <Text style={buttonLabel("secondary")}>Updates</Text>
</Button>
```

### Names for screen readers [#names-for-screen-readers]

A string child is also the button's name for screen readers — they read the text it draws — so `<Button onPress={retry}>Retry</Button>` needs nothing else: a test finds it as `role:button[Retry]`. `accessibilityLabel` still wins when the name should differ from the visible text. Children drawn as given are named by the texts inside them; a button that draws no text needs the `accessibilityLabel` yourself, and an `IconButton` or `RoundButton` (an icon and no text) will not compile without one.

```tsx
<Button onPress={retry}>Retry</Button>
<IconButton accessibilityLabel="Retry the upload" icon={RotateCw} onPress={retry} />
```

### Icon button [#icon-button]

A square icon-only button; `size` takes four: `xs` 20 points across with a pointer (32 on a touch
screen), `sm` 24 (36), `default` 28 (40) and `lg` 32 (44), where a hit slop makes the target 44
points and the icon grows with the square. `lg` is upstream's 32 pt tool square, for a rich text
toolbar; `xs` is a tab's close × beside a document's name. `selected` (a base prop) shows it as
chosen.

`icon` draws a lucide node in the look's size and tint: the chosen surface's ink while selected, the danger tone as
`destructive`; in the terminal, which draws no icons, the `accessibilityLabel` is its text. For an
icon of your own, pass it as `children` and spread `iconButtonGlyph` on it. `iconButtonSizes` is the
table, for geometry that has to match a square. A ghost icon button keeps the scale's metrics (28
points with 12 of padding at `default`, 32 and 16 at `lg`), so a bare square is `IconButton` with
`size="xs"`; a bare text button — a Dock header's Hide — is `size="sm"`; there is no separate bare
variant.

```tsx
<IconButton accessibilityLabel="Star" icon={Star} selected={starred()} onPress={toggle} />
<IconButton accessibilityLabel="Delete" icon={Trash} variant="destructive" onPress={remove} />
```

A tool in a rich text toolbar, at upstream's 32 pt:

```tsx
<IconButton accessibilityLabel="Bold" icon={Bold} size="lg" onPress={bold} />
```

### Round button [#round-button]

`size` is the scale (28 points at `default` with a pointer, 40 on a touch screen); `side` is an exact diameter where the scale is off.

```tsx
<RoundButton accessibilityLabel="Play" onPress={play}>
  <Icon icon={Play} fill {...roundButtonGlyph("default")} />
</RoundButton>
```

### Split button [#split-button]

A main action and a menu half in one silhouette.

```tsx
<SplitButton variant="default">
  <SplitButtonSegment onPress={save}>Save</SplitButtonSegment>
  <SplitButtonDivider />
  <SplitButtonSegment accessibilityLabel="More" onPress={openMenu}>
    <Icon icon={ChevronDown} {...buttonGlyph("default")} />
  </SplitButtonSegment>
</SplitButton>
```

### The look alone [#the-look-alone]

The look is a function, for a pressable of your own.

```tsx
<View onPress={open} {...buttonLook("ghost")}>
  <Text style={buttonLabel("ghost")}>Open</Text>
</View>
```

A ghost button's label that should line up with a card's edge is the same `View` with the look's
padding on its leading side: the look carries `buttonSizes[size].pad` (12 at `default`, 16 at
`lg`), so a `View` with `paddingLeft: buttonSizes.default.pad` around a ghost `Button` moves the
label to the edge and keeps the hover fill the width of the button. The library ships no helper for
it: the padding is the look's own.

## API [#api]

| Part                 | Props                                                                       | Description                                                                     |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Button`             | `variant`, `size`, `icon`, `busy`, `accessibilityLabel`, `children`         | A press that acts; a string child is the label and its name for screen readers. |
| `IconButton`         | `variant`, `size`, `icon`, `accessibilityLabel`, `children`                 | A square icon-only button; it will not compile without an `accessibilityLabel`. |
| `RoundButton`        | `variant`, `size`, `side`, `icon`, `accessibilityLabel`, `children`         | A round icon-only button; `side` is an exact diameter where the scale is off.   |
| `SplitButton`        | `variant`, `size`                                                           | A main action and a menu half in one silhouette.                                |
| `SplitButtonSegment` | every [`nsh/base` Button](https://nsh.dev/elements/button) prop; `children` | One half; a string child is the label and its name for screen readers.          |
| `SplitButtonDivider` | `style`                                                                     | The hairline between the main action and the menu half.                         |

### Button [#button]

Every prop of [`nsh/base` Button](https://nsh.dev/elements/button) passes through. `style`, `hoverStyle`, `activeStyle`, `focusVisibleStyle` and `disabledStyle` go over the look's.

| Prop                 | Type                                                                | Default     |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `variant`            | `"default" \| "secondary" \| "outline" \| "ghost" \| "destructive"` | `"default"` |
| `size`               | `"sm" \| "default" \| "lg"`                                         | `"default"` |
| `icon`               | `IconNode` (lucide)                                                 |             |
| `busy`               | `boolean`                                                           | `false`     |
| `accessibilityLabel` | `string`                                                            |             |
| `children`           | `string \| JSX.Element`                                             |             |

### IconButton [#iconbutton]

| Prop                 | Type                                                   | Default     |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- |
| `variant`            | `"ghost" \| "secondary" \| "outline" \| "destructive"` | `"ghost"`   |
| `size`               | `"xs" \| "sm" \| "default" \| "lg"`                    | `"default"` |
| `icon`               | `IconNode` (lucide)                                    |             |
| `accessibilityLabel` | `string` (required: an icon names nothing)             |
| `children`           | `JSX.Element`                                          |             |

`selected` (a base prop) shows it as chosen. `iconButtonSizes` is the table: `side`, the square's
side in points, and `glyph`, the icon's size.

### RoundButton [#roundbutton]

| Prop                 | Type                                       | Default     |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------- |
| `variant`            | `"default" \| "secondary"`                 | `"default"` |
| `size`               | `"sm" \| "default" \| "lg"`                | `"default"` |
| `side`               | `number`                                   |             |
| `icon`               | `IconNode` (lucide)                        |             |
| `accessibilityLabel` | `string` (required: an icon names nothing) |
| `children`           | `JSX.Element`                              |             |

### SplitButton [#splitbutton]

| Prop      | Type                                                                | Default     |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `variant` | `"default" \| "secondary" \| "outline" \| "ghost" \| "destructive"` | `"default"` |
| `size`    | `"sm" \| "default" \| "lg"`                                         | `"default"` |

`SplitButtonSegment` takes every prop of [`nsh/base` Button](https://nsh.dev/elements/button); a string child is the label, and its name for screen readers.

# Calendar (/dev/docs/components/calendar)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add calendar
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Calendar } from "@/components/ui/calendar";
```

```tsx
<Calendar value={value} onChange={({ value }) => setValue(value)} />
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Controlled [#controlled]

```tsx
<Calendar value={day()} onChange={({ value }) => day.set(value)} />
```

`value` is an ISO date; with `range` it is `[start, end]`. While the second end is chosen, the band
previews the range from the first to a later day under the pointer or the keyboard; the pick
commits it. A day before the first starts the range again, so nothing is previewed there.

### Uncontrolled [#uncontrolled]

Without `value` the calendar keeps its own, starting at `defaultValue`.

```tsx
<Calendar defaultValue="2026-11-11" onChange={({ value }) => save(value)} />
```

## API [#api]

Defaults from `calendarLook` / `CalendarItem`. Every prop of [`nsh/base` Calendar](https://nsh.dev/elements/calendar) passes through.

| Part           | Props                                                  | Description                                                                            |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Calendar`     | `value`, `defaultValue`, `onChange`, `range`           | A month of days to pick a date or a range, on the shared calendar look.                |
| `CalendarItem` | `item` (a `CalendarEntry`), `months`, `firstDayOfWeek` | One day of the grid (a square in `shape.control`); what `renderItem` draws by default. |

# Card (/dev/docs/components/card)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add card
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import {
  Card,
  CardAction,
  CardContent,
  CardDescription,
  CardFooter,
  CardHeader,
  CardTitle,
} from "@/components/ui/card";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <CardHeader>
    <CardTitle>Login to your account</CardTitle>
    <CardDescription>Enter your email below to login to your account.</CardDescription>
    <CardAction>
      <Button variant="ghost">Sign up</Button>
    </CardAction>
  </CardHeader>
  <CardContent>
    <Input placeholder="m@example.com" />
  </CardContent>
  <CardFooter>
    <Button>Login</Button>
  </CardFooter>
</Card>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Card`:

```text
Card
├── CardHeader
│   ├── CardTitle
│   ├── CardDescription
│   └── CardAction
├── CardContent
└── CardFooter
```

## Examples [#examples]

### With a form [#with-a-form]

`CardContent` pads its sides and nothing else: space the fields the way the form needs.

```tsx
<Card>
  <CardHeader>
    <CardTitle>Payment method</CardTitle>
    <CardDescription>All transactions are secure and encrypted.</CardDescription>
  </CardHeader>
  <CardContent>
    <View style={{ gap: 10 }}>
      <Field>
        <FieldLabel>Name on card</FieldLabel>
        <Input placeholder="Evil Rabbit" />
      </Field>
      <Field>
        <FieldLabel>Card number</FieldLabel>
        <Input placeholder="1234 5678 9012 3456" />
      </Field>
    </View>
  </CardContent>
  <CardFooter>
    <Button>Pay</Button>
  </CardFooter>
</Card>
```

### Two side by side [#two-side-by-side]
