| Part     | Props           | Description                                                                       |
| -------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Status` | `label`, `tone` | A dot and a word, 12 points; a tone that matters tints both, neutral stays quiet. |

# Switch (/dev/docs/components/switch)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add switch
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Switch } from "@/components/ui/switch";
```

```tsx
<Switch checked={on()} onChange={({ checked }) => on.set(checked)}>
  Wi-Fi
</Switch>
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Size [#size]

`size` switches between the theme's standard (`default`) and compact (`sm`) switch geometry in `switch.*` and `switch.small.*` (with pointer vs touch scales applied automatically via the active input `tier`; WinUI 3 uses `44 × 22` / `sm 36 × 18` on touch).

```tsx
<Switch size="sm" checked={on()} onChange={({ checked }) => on.set(checked)} />
<Switch size="default" checked={on()} onChange={({ checked }) => on.set(checked)} />
```

### Disabled [#disabled]

```tsx
<Switch checked={false} disabled>
  <Text>Ask to join networks</Text>
</Switch>
```

### In a row [#in-a-row]

A row with its label is the target: put the label in `children` and let `listRow` draw the row.

```tsx
<Switch
  checked={wifi()}
  onChange={({ checked }) => wifi.set(checked)}
  {...listRow({ first: true, style: { flexDirection: "row-reverse" } })}
>
  <RowDivider show={false} />
  <RowLabel label="Wi-Fi" />
</Switch>
```

A switch is the whole row here — its children are its label, so a tap anywhere on the row toggles it — and it is read as a switch that is on or off, because `Switch` sets its own role and its own value. Nothing else has to say either.

### A settings row [#a-settings-row]

A `Field` in a row puts a title and its description at the start, `FieldContent` takes the room
the control leaves, and the switch sits after them.

```tsx
<Field orientation="horizontal">
  <FieldContent>
    <FieldLabel>Extract text from images</FieldLabel>
    <FieldDescription>Read the text in a screenshot you paste or open.</FieldDescription>
  </FieldContent>
  <Switch
    accessibilityLabel="Extract text from images"
    checked={extract()}
    onChange={({ checked }) => extract.set(checked)}
  />
</Field>
```

The title is beside the switch, not in it, so the switch carries the row's name in `accessibilityLabel`; it is still read as that switch and its state. A list of them is a `FieldGroup`, and `FieldSeparator` draws the hairline between two rows.

A title beside a switch takes no presses, so the switch is the target — a touch screen gives it the room a finger needs (`hitSlop`) — and a row that should toggle on a tap anywhere is the `listRow` row above.

Nothing in the row names a side: `Field` lays its children out along the writing direction, so a right-to-left app puts the switch first and the text against the other edge, with the row unchanged.

```tsx
<View style={{ direction: "rtl" }}>
  <Field orientation="horizontal">…the same row…</Field>
</View>
```

### Alone [#alone]

With no children the track is all of it; a touch screen raises the target to 44 points, and the track
is already at least that wide, so the hit slop only fills the height.

```tsx
<Switch
  accessibilityLabel="Bluetooth"
  checked={bluetooth()}
  onChange={({ checked }) => bluetooth.set(checked)}
/>
```

### The look alone [#the-look-alone]

`switchLook` gives the track and knob classes to a `nsh/base` switch of your own; `switchHitSlop` gives the touch target.

```tsx
<BaseSwitch
  {...switchLook(() => on(), "default")}
  checked={on()}
  onChange={({ checked }) => on.set(checked)}
/>
```

The settings row's looks are the field family's, for a `nsh/base` view of your own:

```tsx
<View style={fieldFamilyLook().field(true)}>
  <View style={fieldFamilyLook().content}>
    <Text style={fieldFamilyLook().title}>Extract text from images</Text>
    <Text style={fieldFamilyLook().description}>Read the text in a screenshot.</Text>
  </View>
  <BaseSwitch {...switchLook(() => on())} checked={on()} />
</View>
```

Each part of `fieldFamilyLook()` reads the theme when it is drawn, so a look kept in a `const` still follows the scheme.

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh/base` Switch](https://nsh.dev/elements/switch) passes through. `trackClass`, `trackStyle` and `thumbStyle` go over the look's.

| Part     | Props                                                                                                                    | Description                                                                                                                       |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Switch` | `checked`, `onChange`, `size`, `disabled`, `children`, `accessibilityLabel`, `hitSlop`, and every `nsh/base` Switch prop | An on / off switch; alone it fills the touch target's height with a hit slop, with children it is a row whose label is the target |

### Where the numbers come from [#where-the-numbers-come-from]

The track, border (`switch.edge.off`, `switch.edge.on`, `switch.edge.color`), knob dimensions (`switch.track`, `switch.knob.*`), and derived press feedback all read `controls().switch` (`packages/ui/lib/look.ts`) so switching themes updates geometry and motion on the next frame:

- **Apple** draws an oval knob on a borderless pill track (`54 × 24` with `31 × 20` knob on pointer; `63 × 28` with `37 × 24` on touch; `sm`: `40 × 18` with `23 × 14` on pointer).
- **shadcn** draws a borderless pill track (`32 × 18` on pointer, `sm`: `24 × 14`; `44 × 24` / `36 × 20` on touch) with `--input` off track.
- **Material 3** draws a `40 × 24` (`52 × 32` touch; `sm`: `32 × 20` / `40 × 24`) track with an `outline` border when off and an expanding circle knob (`16 → 20 / 24` on, `22 / 28` pressed; `sm`: `12pt` rest).
- **WinUI 3** draws a `40 × 20` (`44 × 22` touch; `sm`: `32 × 16` / `36 × 18` touch) track with a strong off border (`ControlStrongStrokeColorDefault`) and a `12pt` (`14pt` touch; `sm`: `10pt` / `12pt`) circle knob that enlarges on hover and stretches while pressed.

A standalone switch adds `focusRing()` shaped to the capsule track and handles disabled appearance directly (dimming via `dimmed.disabled` when `controls.disabled.face` is `keep`, or switching to `disabled.*` surface/ink/edge on Material 3 and WinUI 3).

### Sizes [#sizes]

| Size      | Track (`nsh-gallery` / `solid-glass`)      | Knob      |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------ | --------- |
| `default` | `icon.md` + 4 high, 2 × `icon.md` + 4 long | `icon.md` |
| `sm`      | `icon.sm` + 4 high, 2 × `icon.sm` + 4 long | `icon.sm` |

In `nsh-gallery` and `solid-glass`, that is 36 × 20 with a 16-point knob under a pointer and 44 × 24 with 20 on a touch screen (`sm`: 28 × 16 with 12, 36 × 20 with 16): 2 points of track above, below and at each end, so the knob travels its own width — as far from the end on as off.

`SwitchSize` is `"sm" | "default"`.

Off, the knob wears `finish.knob`; on, it reads `finish.knob.checkedBackground` / `checkedBorderColor` / `checkedGradient` (`packages/ui/switch.tsx`, `knobLook`).

# Table (/dev/docs/components/table)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add table
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import {
  Table,
  TableBody,
  TableCell,
  TableHead,
  TableHeader,
  TableRow,
} from "@/components/ui/table";
```

```tsx
<Table accessibilityLabel="Invoices">
  <TableHeader>
    <TableRow>
      <TableHead>Invoice</TableHead>
      <TableHead>Status</TableHead>
    </TableRow>
  </TableHeader>
  <TableBody>
    <TableRow selected>
      <TableCell>INV001</TableCell>
      <TableCell>Paid</TableCell>
    </TableRow>
  </TableBody>
</Table>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Table`:

```text
Table
├── TableCaption
├── TableHeader
│   └── TableRow
│       └── TableHead
├── TableBody
│   └── TableRow
│       └── TableCell
└── TableFooter
    └── TableRow
        └── TableCell
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Selected row [#selected-row]

`TableRow` accepts `selected` for the `rowSelected` fill.

### String children [#string-children]

`TableHead`, `TableCell`, and `TableCaption` render strings with muted or foreground text.

## API [#api]

| Part           | Props                          | Description                                                                    |
| -------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Table`        | every `nsh/base` Table prop    | The app's rows as a bordered card; screen readers hear the base roles          |
| `TableHeader`  | base props                     | The header band                                                                |
| `TableBody`    | base props                     | The body group                                                                 |
| `TableFooter`  | base props                     | The footer band, a hairline above                                              |
| `TableRow`     | base props, `selected`         | A row with a hairline above; `selected` fills it with the look's `rowSelected` |
| `TableHead`    | `children` (string or element) | A column's header cell; a string is drawn in the quiet header text             |
| `TableCell`    | `children`                     | A body or footer cell; a string is drawn in the body text                      |
| `TableCaption` | `children`                     | The caption under the rows; a string is drawn muted                            |

`tableRowClass` is the row's color transition, for a row of your own.

# Tabs (/dev/docs/components/tabs)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add tabs
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Tabs, TabsContent, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@/components/ui/tabs";
```

```tsx
<Tabs defaultValue="overview">
  <TabsList>
    <TabsTrigger value="overview">Overview</TabsTrigger>
  </TabsList>
  <TabsContent value="overview">…</TabsContent>
</Tabs>
```

The pill track is as wide as its tabs, the tabs as wide as their labels; an underline is as wide as
its labels and its rule. A touch screen always spans the row, and `fill` spans it with a pointer.

The chosen tab is a plate on the track — the theme's `plate`, a labelled block inside the well —
and a tab's own box is that plate's box, so the pointer's hover shade covers exactly where the pill
is.

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Tabs`:

```text
Tabs
├── TabsList
│   └── TabsTrigger
└── TabsContent
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Underline [#underline]

```tsx
<TabsList variant="line">
  <TabsTrigger value="inbox">Inbox</TabsTrigger>
</TabsList>
```

### Spanning the row [#spanning-the-row]

```tsx
<TabsList fill>
  <TabsTrigger value="overview">Overview</TabsTrigger>
  <TabsTrigger value="activity">Activity</TabsTrigger>
</TabsList>
```

## API [#api]

| Part          | Props                                                       | Description                                                                                                         |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Tabs`        | `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange`, `orientation`     | Holds the selected value and lays its list and panel out                                                            |
| `TabsList`    | `variant`, `fill`, and every `nsh/base` Tabs prop           | The tablist: `default` the pill track of `tabsLook`, `line` the underlined strip; as wide as its tabs unless `fill` |
| `TabsTrigger` | `value`, and every `nsh/base` Tab prop                      | One tab; a string child is its label, drawn with `TabTitle`                                                         |
| `TabsContent` | `value`                                                     | The panel for one value, hidden (not unmounted) while another is selected                                           |
| `TabTitle`    | `name`, `selected`, `count`, `icon`, `underline`, `onWidth` | The label to pair with a tab: the icon's two tints crossing over, a count in a capsule                              |

Every prop of [`nsh/base` Tabs / `Tab`](https://nsh.dev/elements/tabs) passes through on the list and triggers.

# Terminal (/dev/docs/components/terminal)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add terminal
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Terminal, type TerminalRef } from "@/components/ui/terminal";
```

```tsx
let term: TerminalRef | undefined;

<Terminal
  ref={(r) => (term = r)}
  accessibilityLabel="Shell"
  onData={({ data }) => program.write(data)}
  onResize={({ cols, rows }) => program.resize(cols, rows)}
/>;
```

The terminal starts nothing: `term.write(bytes)` shows what the program printed, `onData` carries what the user typed or pasted (keys the program expects, the emulator's answers included), and `onResize` reports the size in cells. `term.reset()` clears the screen and the scrollback, `term.text()` gives every line, `term.focus()` takes the keyboard.

## Examples [#examples]

### A terminal in the page [#a-terminal-in-the-page]

The default: a well of the field's fill and edge, the theme's inner corners and a padding, so a
terminal sits beside the other controls.

```tsx
<Terminal ref={(r) => (term = r)} accessibilityLabel="Shell" style={{ height: 320 }} />
```

### An app whose window is the terminal [#an-app-whose-window-is-the-terminal]

`variant="ghost"` draws no fill, no edge, no padding and no corners: the app's own surface is the
frame, and the terminal covers it.

```tsx
<View class="bg-background flex-1">
  <Terminal variant="ghost" ref={(r) => (term = r)} accessibilityLabel="Shell" class="flex-1" />
</View>
```

### A real program [#a-real-program]

A terminal is a stream of bytes in and out; the app owns both ends.

- **On the desktop**, a pseudo-terminal: the app spawns the shell in a pty (`portable-pty` in Rust,
  a native pty module in TypeScript), reads the master side into `term.write(chunk)` and sends
  `onData`'s payload back to it. The size `onResize` reports is the pty's window size.
- **On the web**, a WebSocket to a shell service: `socket.onmessage` writes the socket's bytes,
  `onData` and `onResize` send them the other way.
- **A remote session** (`ssh`, a container's exec stream) fills the same two directions.

Nothing of that is the terminal's: it interprets the escape sequences it is given and draws them
with the platform's text engine. NSH's [Terminal](https://nsh.dev/elements/terminal) documents the
escape sequences it understands and how a Rust app replaces the emulator (`TerminalEmulatorFactory`).

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh/base` Terminal](https://nsh.dev/elements/terminal) passes through, and so does
its ref (`TerminalRef`): `write`, `reset`, `text`, `focus`. `class`, `style`, `cursorClass` and
`cursorStyle` go over the look's, so an app gives the cursor its shape (`w-0.5`) and moves the
padding where it needs another.

The 16 ANSI colors are NSH's own palette; text a program leaves uncolored is the theme's
`foreground`, and cells it leaves without a background show the terminal's own surface.

| Part       | Props                                                                                                      | Description                                                                                |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Terminal` | `variant`, and every `nsh/base` Terminal prop (`onData`, `onResize`, `style`, …); the ref is `TerminalRef` | A program's output on the theme's field surface; `variant="ghost"` draws no surface at all |

# TextView (/dev/docs/components/text-view)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add text-view
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { TextView, textViewCaretClass, textViewLinkClasses } from "@/components/ui/text-view";
```

```tsx
<TextView markdown={doc} />

<TextView
  markdown={streamingDoc}
  streamingCaret={<View class={textViewCaretClass} />}
/>
```

`TextView` merges `textViewLinkClasses` into `classes` by default.

## Examples [#examples]

### Markdown [#markdown]

```tsx
<TextView markdown={"See the [guide](https://example.com).\n\n> A short note."} />
```

### Streaming [#streaming]

`streamingCaret` marks the end of text still arriving; `textViewCaretClass` is the caret's look.

```tsx
<TextView markdown={streamingDoc} streamingCaret={<View class={textViewCaretClass} />} />
```

### Copy on code blocks [#copy-on-code-blocks]

`codeBlockActions` puts buttons over each code block's top-right corner: ghost buttons that show
while a pointer hovers the block on a desktop and always on a touch screen. The `copy` action is
built in — it copies the block's code and shows a check for a moment — so a reply with a command
needs nothing more. Other ids are the app's: they are drawn with `renderCodeBlockAction`'s icon and
their press arrives at `onCodeBlockAction`.

````tsx
const GIT = "```sh\nnsh export --out backup.json\n```";

<TextView markdown={GIT} codeBlockActions={[{ id: "copy", label: "Copy code" }]} />;
````

The built-in copy's accessibility label is the action's `label`; give an app action its own
`renderCodeBlockAction` and handle `id` in `onCodeBlockAction`.

### A block of your own [#a-block-of-your-own]

An extension claims a Markdown shape for the app. A `language` claims a fence; `renderCustom`
receives the node, with `node.text` the fence's source, and returns the view to draw in its place.
Here a `chart` fence lists `label value` lines and becomes bars in the theme's brand color.

````tsx
const CHART_EXTENSIONS = [{ name: "chart", language: "chart" }];

function Chart(props: { source: string }) {
  const bars = props.source
    .trim()
    .split("\n")
    .map((line) => {
      const [label, raw] = line.trim().split(/\s+/);
      return { label, value: Number(raw) || 0 };
    });
  const max = Math.max(1, ...bars.map((bar) => bar.value));
  return (
    <View
      style={{
        height: 132,
        flexDirection: "row",
        alignItems: "flex-end",
        gap: 8,
        padding: 12,
        borderWidth: 1,
        borderColor: colors.line,
        borderRadius: 12,
        backgroundColor: colors.inset,
      }}
    >
      <Each of={bars} key={(bar) => bar.label}>
        {(bar) => (
          <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", gap: 4 }}>
            <Text style={{ fontSize: 11, color: colors.faint }}>{bar().value}</Text>
            <View
              style={{
                width: "100%",
                height: Math.max(4, Math.round((bar().value / max) * 64)),
                borderRadius: 6,
                backgroundColor: colors.brand,
              }}
            />
            <Text style={{ fontSize: 11, color: colors.mutedForeground }}>{bar().label}</Text>
          </View>
        )}
      </Each>
    </View>
  );
}

<TextView
  markdown={"```chart\nInstall 12\nBuild 34\nTest 21\nShip 8\n```"}
  extensions={CHART_EXTENSIONS}
  renderCustom={(node) => <Chart source={node.text ?? ""} />}
/>;
````

A `pattern` claims inline text instead (the next example), and `tag` and `container` claim a tag
or a wrapping block. `renderCustom` is called for every custom node in the document, so branch on
`node.name` when the app claims more than one shape.

### Inline chips [#inline-chips]

An inline extension replaces each match of its `pattern` with the node the app draws. Keep the
chip's `verticalAlign` at `middle` and its height under the line height, so the paragraph's lines
keep their spacing; `styles.root.lineHeight` gives the chip the room it needs.

```tsx
const CHIPS =
  "The install broke on T-0089 after nsh#810 and both were fixed in nsh#812 before T-0091 followed.";
const CHIP_EXTENSIONS = [
  { name: "task", pattern: "\\bT-\\d{4}\\b" },
  { name: "pr", pattern: "\\b[a-z-]+#\\d+\\b" },
];

<TextView
  markdown={CHIPS}
  extensions={CHIP_EXTENSIONS}
  styles={{ root: { fontSize: 17, lineHeight: 26 } }}
  renderCustom={(node) => (
    <View class="border-border bg-inset h-5 flex-row items-center gap-1.5 rounded-full border px-2 align-middle">
      <View
        class={
          node.name === "task" ? "bg-info size-1.5 rounded-full" : "bg-up size-1.5 rounded-full"
        }
      />
      <Text class="font-mono text-[13px] leading-4">{node.text}</Text>
    </View>
  )}
/>;
```

### Images that open [#images-that-open]

`onImagePress` reports the image that was pressed as `{ src, alt }`: the shape [`ImageViewer`](./image-viewer) takes. Hold it in a signal, and the viewer is open while it is set.

```tsx
const viewing = signal<ImageViewerImage | null>(null);

<TextView markdown={markdown} onImagePress={({ image }) => viewing.set(image)} />
<ImageViewer image={viewing()} onClose={() => viewing.set(null)} />;
```

## API [#api]

`TextView.parse`, `parseHtml`, and `plainText` are re-exported from base. Every prop of [`nsh/base` TextView](https://nsh.dev/elements/text-view) passes through.

| Part                                       | Props                                     | Description                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TextView`                                 | every `nsh/base` TextView prop; `classes` | A Markdown, HTML or block document; `classes` merges over `textViewLinkClasses` |
| `TextView.parse`, `parseHtml`, `plainText` | base's parsers                            | A document, parsed ahead of drawing                                             |
| `textViewLinkClasses`                      | `{ link }`                                | The link classes the view merges in: the brand color over a faint underline     |
| `textViewCaretClass`                       | —                                         | The streaming caret: a brand block a line high, pulsing                         |

# Time Field (/dev/docs/components/time-field)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm

```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx

```

```tsx
<TimeField value={time()} onChange={({ value }) => value && time.set(value)} />
```

## Examples [#examples]

### The look alone [#the-look-alone]

```tsx
<TimeField class={timeFieldClass()} value={time()} />
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh/base` TimeField](https://nsh.dev/elements/time-field) passes through; `class`, `segmentClass`, `separatorStyle` and `renderSegment` go over the look's.

| Part             | Props                                                    | Description                                                                           |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TimeField`      | `value`, `onChange`, and every `nsh/base` TimeField prop | A time of day, one segment at a time, in the input's well and the calendar's segments |

# TitleBar (/dev/docs/components/title-bar)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add title-bar
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Text } from "nsh";

import {
  TITLE_BAR_HEIGHT,
  TitleBar,
  WindowControls,
  WindowResizeEdges,
} from "@/components/ui/title-bar";
```

A desktop window with `titleBar: { style: "hidden" }` keeps the system's window buttons and leaves
the rest of the bar to the app: `TitleBar` draws it, drags the window, and pads its children clear
of the buttons (`titleBar()`'s `left` and `right`).

```tsx
<TitleBar>
  {/* the app's own: a logo, the document's name, a search field, a button */}
  <Text style={{ flex: 1 }}>Notes.nsh</Text>
</TitleBar>
```

`TitleBar` draws nothing where the app has no window of its own — a browser page, a phone — and
`WindowControls` are inert there: the bar is a window's, and there is none.

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `TitleBar`:

```text
TitleBar
├── WindowControls
└── WindowResizeEdges
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Traffic lights [#traffic-lights]

A window with `frame: "none"` has no title bar and no border: the app draws the bar, the lights
and the edges itself. `WindowControls` puts the platform's three buttons at the leading end, the
app's own content after them.

```tsx
<View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  <TitleBar>
    <WindowControls />
    <Text style={{ flex: 1 }}>Time sheet.nsh</Text>
  </TitleBar>
  <View style={{ flex: 1 }}>{document}</View>
  <WindowResizeEdges />
</View>
```

The glyphs are drawn while the pointer is over the lights, as the system draws them, and the
lights turn grey while the window is in the background.

### Caption buttons [#caption-buttons]

Windows' and Linux's buttons are cells at the trailing end of the bar, filling its height.
They sit flush against the window's corner, so the bar's trailing padding goes to zero:

```tsx
<TitleBar style={{ paddingEnd: 0 }}>
  <Text style={{ flex: 1 }}>Notes.nsh</Text>
  <WindowControls variant="caption" />
</TitleBar>
```

### Your own window controls [#your-own-window-controls]

The three parts are the shapes the platforms draw; an app that wants its own draws the same
`desktop` views itself, and the platform still carries out the press. A round close button
(`Icon` from `lib/ui/icons`, `lightInk` from `lib/ui/title-bar`, `X` from `lucide`; the
traffic lights keep macOS's own hues whatever the theme, so the disc's colour is written out
rather than read from a role):

```tsx
<View
  desktop={{ windowControl: "close" }}
  role="button"
  accessibilityLabel="Close"
  style={{
    width: 28,
    height: 28,
    borderRadius: 14,
    alignItems: "center",
    justifyContent: "center",
  }}
  hoverStyle={{ backgroundColor: "#FF5F57" }}
>
  <Icon icon={X} size={12} tint={lightInk} />
</View>
```

A bar of the app's own takes `desktop={{ windowDrag: true }}` to drag the window, and pads by
`titleBar().left` and `titleBar().right` so its content clears the system's buttons.

## API [#api]

| Part                | Props                                                               | Description                                 |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `TitleBar`          | every `nsh` View prop; look `titleBarLook().root()`                 | The bar that drags the window               |
| `WindowControls`    | `variant`; every `nsh` View prop; look `titleBarLook().controls(…)` | The window's own buttons                    |
| `WindowResizeEdges` | look `titleBarLook().resize(edge)`                                  | The edges and corners of a frameless window |

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through on all three, and `style`
goes over the look's on `TitleBar` and `WindowControls`.

| Prop      | Type                            | Default          |
| --------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| `variant` | `"traffic-lights" \| "caption"` | `traffic-lights` |

`TitleBar` is `TITLE_BAR_HEIGHT` (40 points) tall, or the height the system's title bar has, on
the inset fill with a hairline under it; its children start `12` points after the system's buttons.
A traffic light is `TRAFFIC_LIGHT` (12 points) wide, in macOS's own close, minimize and zoom hues wherever the theme goes (`lightTone`, with glyphs in `lightInk` and the disc's `lightEdge`), and `CAPTION_BUTTON` (46) is a caption cell's width; the close cell
washes the destructive tint while the pointer is on it. `WindowResizeEdges` draws eight strips —
`5` points along the edges, `12` at the corners — as the last child of the window's root.
`titleBarLook()` is exported for a bar the app lays out itself.

# Toast (/dev/docs/components/toast)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add toast
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { toast, Toaster } from "@/components/ui/toast";
```

```tsx
toast("Copied", { description: "The link is on the clipboard." });

// Once, at the root.
<Toaster />;
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Action [#action]

```tsx
<Toast>
  <Text style={toastTitle()}>Deleted</Text>
  <Button {...toastActionLook()}>
    <Text style={toastActionLabel()}>Undo</Text>
  </Button>
</Toast>
```

### From code [#from-code]

`toast` follows sonner. It returns an id. The same id replaces the toast that held it. `update` changes one where it is, which is how a loading note becomes its result — sonner does that by calling `toast` again with the same id, and this queue also has `toast.update` so the entrance does not restart. `progress` (0 to 1) is the bar under the text; sonner has none.

```tsx
const id = toast.loading("Uploading 3 photos", {
  description: "0 of 3",
  progress: 0,
  duration: Infinity,
});
toast.update(id, { progress: 1, type: "success", title: "3 photos uploaded", duration: 4000 });
toast.dismiss(id);
```

An action's `onClick` runs when it is pressed, and `onDismiss` hears that action's label — or `null` when the toast leaves any other way.

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh/base` Toast](https://nsh.dev/elements/toast) passes through. `style` goes over `toastLook`.

| Part            | Props                                                                                     | Description                                                                            |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Toast`         | `title`, `description`, `children`, and every `nsh/base` Toast prop                       | A raised banner; without children it draws `title` and `description`                   |
| `toast`         | `(title, options?)` → `string`                                                            | Shows one. `success`, `error`, `warning`, `info`, `loading` set `type`                 |
| `options`       | `id`, `description`, `duration`, `type`, `action`, `closeButton`, `progress`, `onDismiss` | `duration` defaults to 4000; `Infinity` stays. `closeButton: true` is labelled "Close" |
| `toast.update`  | `(id, change) → boolean`                                                                  | Changes a toast in place. `null` clears `description`, `action` or `progress`          |
| `toast.dismiss` | `(id?)`                                                                                   | Closes one toast, or every toast when `id` is omitted                                  |
| `Toaster`       |                                                                                           | The stack at the foot of the window. Mount it once                                     |

`toastLook`, `toastTitle`, `toastText`, `toastCloseLook`, `toastActionLook` and `toastActionLabel` are the look's parts, for content of your own.

# Toggle (/dev/docs/components/toggle)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add toggle
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Toggle, ToggleGroup } from "@/components/ui/toggle";
```

```tsx
<Toggle pressed={on()} onChange={({ pressed }) => on.set(pressed)}>
  Bold
</Toggle>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Toggle`:

```text
Toggle

ToggleGroup
└── Toggle
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Variant [#variant]

```tsx
<Toggle>Bold</Toggle>
<Toggle variant="outline">Bold</Toggle>
```

### Size [#size]

```tsx
<Toggle size="sm">Small</Toggle>
<Toggle size="default">Default</Toggle>
<Toggle size="lg">Large</Toggle>
```

A size is a step of the theme's own scales: its `side` the three heights (`dimension.size.height`),
its `icon` the three icons (`dimension.icon`), its label the `detail`, `body` and `label` type roles.
The NSH Gallery theme's heights are 24 / 28 / 32 points with a pointer and 32 / 40 / 48 on a touch
screen, where a hit slop makes the target 44 points.

### Disabled [#disabled]

`disabled` on a `Toggle` locks that one. `disabled` on a `ToggleGroup` locks every toggle in it —
the base bar hands its lock down, so no child needs its own `disabled`. A disabled toggle takes no
press, leaves the arrow keys' walk and reads as disabled to screen readers; it dims to 50%
(`disabledStyle`).

```tsx
<Toggle disabled>Bold</Toggle>
<ToggleGroup disabled>
  <Toggle pressed={bold()}>B</Toggle>
  <Toggle pressed={italic()}>I</Toggle>
</ToggleGroup>
```

### Group [#group]

A group is one toolbar for screen readers: one stop of the keyboard focus, arrow keys between its toggles. The default wears the inset track.

```tsx
<ToggleGroup>
  <Toggle pressed={bold()} onChange={({ pressed }) => bold.set(pressed)}>
    Bold
  </Toggle>
</ToggleGroup>
```

### Vertical [#vertical]

```tsx
<ToggleGroup vertical>
  <Toggle pressed={bold()}>Bold</Toggle>
</ToggleGroup>
```

### Inside a Toolbar [#inside-a-toolbar]

```tsx
import { Toolbar } from "@/components/ui/toolbar";

<Toolbar>
  <ToggleGroup inset={false}>
    <Toggle pressed={bold()}>B</Toggle>
  </ToggleGroup>
</Toolbar>;
```

`inset={false}` skips the track when a parent `Toolbar` already wears it.

### Chips [#chips]

A row of single-select capsules is a recipe, not a part. shadcn/ui has no capsule axis on `ToggleGroup`; where it wants one it puts `rounded-full` on the items. Here the same call-site `style` does it: `inset={false}` drops the track, `gap` spaces the chips, and `borderRadius: 999` makes the capsule. A capsule is geometry, not a theme role (`shape.control` is the corner of a badge), so the radius is the full one. The base group holds no value: the app presses the chip asked for and keeps the chosen one pressed. For a row that scrolls, put the group in a horizontal `Scroll`.

```tsx
<ToggleGroup inset={false} style={{ gap: 8, flexWrap: "wrap", maxWidth: "100%" }}>
  <Toggle
    variant="outline"
    size="lg"
    pressed={chip() === "Orbit"}
    style={{ borderRadius: 999 }}
    onChange={({ pressed }) => pressed && chip.set("Orbit")}
  >
    Orbit
  </Toggle>
</ToggleGroup>
```

### Pressed [#pressed]

```tsx
<Toggle pressed={on()} onChange={({ pressed }) => on.set(pressed)}>
  Bold
</Toggle>
```

### Names for screen readers [#names-for-screen-readers]

A string child is the toggle's name for screen readers, and `accessibilityLabel` wins when it should differ from the visible label. Children drawn as given (an icon and a label of your own) are named by the texts inside them.

### The look alone [#the-look-alone]

The look is a function, for a pressable of your own.

```tsx
<Toggle pressed={on()} {...toggleLook({ text: true })}>
  <Text style={toggleLabel(on, { text: true })}>Bold</Text>
</Toggle>
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh/base` Toggle](https://nsh.dev/elements/toggle) and ToggleGroup passes through. `style`, `hoverStyle`, `activeStyle`, `focusVisibleStyle`, `pressedStyle` and `disabledStyle` go over the look's.

| Part          | Props                                                                                               | Description                                                              |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Toggle`      | `variant`, `size`, `children`, and every `nsh/base` Toggle prop (`pressed`, `onChange`, `disabled`) | A two-state button; a string child is its name for screen readers        |
| `ToggleGroup` | `vertical`, `inset`, and every `nsh/base` ToggleGroup prop                                          | The inset track of `toolbarTrack` holding a row (or column) of `Toggle`s |

`toggleLook`, `toggleLabel` and `toggleGlyph` are the look's parts, for a pressable of your own.
`toggleSizes` is the table a size reads — `side`, `icon` and `text` from the theme's height, icon and
type scales, its `pad` the toggle's own (compact with a pointer, roomier on a touch screen) — so a
bar's own geometry can match a tool's (`toggleSizes.default.side`).

# Toolbar (/dev/docs/components/toolbar)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add toolbar
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Toolbar, ToolbarGroup, ToolbarSeparator } from "@/components/ui/toolbar";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar accessibilityLabel="Formatting">
  <ToolbarGroup>
    <Toggle pressed={bold()}>B</Toggle>
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarGroup>
    <Toggle pressed={align() === "left"}>L</Toggle>
  </ToolbarGroup>
</Toolbar>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Toolbar`:

```text
Toolbar
├── ToolbarGroup
│   └── ToolbarButton
├── ToolbarButton
├── ToolbarSeparator
└── ToolbarOverflow
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Disabled [#disabled]

`disabled` on a `Toolbar` locks the whole bar: no item takes a press, the arrows skip it and it is
one disabled toolbar to screen readers. `disabled` on a `ToolbarGroup` locks that run alone, the
rest of the bar still reached. Every item the bar knows locks — a `Button`, a `Toggle`, a `Link`,
a menu's or popover's trigger — because the base bar hands its lock down to each
(`nsh-base/src/toolbar.rs`, "items"). A control that is not a bar item keeps its own `disabled`
and its own behavior inside a locked bar: a `Command` palette, a text field.

```tsx
<Toolbar accessibilityLabel="Formatting" disabled>
  <ToolbarGroup>
    <Toggle pressed={bold()}>B</Toggle>
    <Toggle pressed={italic()}>I</Toggle>
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <Button variant="ghost">Undo</Button>
</Toolbar>
```

### Vertical [#vertical]

```tsx
<Toolbar axis="vertical" accessibilityLabel="Tools">
  <Toggle pressed={tool() === "pen"}>✎</Toggle>
</Toolbar>
```

### The look alone [#the-look-alone]

```tsx
import { Toolbar, ToolbarSeparator, toolbarRule } from "@/components/ui/toolbar";
import { toolbarTrack } from "@/lib/ui/tool";

<Toolbar style={toolbarTrack()}>
  <ToolbarSeparator style={toolbarRule()} />
</Toolbar>;
```

### A formatting bar [#a-formatting-bar]

The bar a text editor puts over the text it formats: history, the block, the marks, the alignment,
a hairline between the runs. Undo and Redo are `Button`s that gray out at the ends of the history;
the marks a `ToggleGroup`; the alignment `Toggle`s that only ever set. The block is a `Menu` whose
**trigger is one of the bar's items** — a `View` inside `MenuTrigger`, which `nsh/base` hands the
press, the focus and the expanded state, so the arrow keys reach it like any other tool and Space or
Return opens it. Give that view `role="button"`, a name and `accessibilityState` and it reads like
the menu button it is. The menu's rows are `MenuRadioItem`s: one block is chosen at a time.

```tsx
const doc = signal({ marks: ["bold"], align: "left", block: "Paragraph" });
const past = signal([]);
const future = signal([]);
const commit = (next, what) => {
  past.set([...past(), doc()].slice(-20));
  future.set([]);
  doc.set({ ...doc(), ...next });
};

<Toolbar accessibilityLabel="Formatting" style={toolbarTrack()}>
  <ToolbarGroup accessibilityLabel="History">
    <Button
      variant="ghost"
      icon={Undo2}
      accessibilityLabel="Undo"
      disabled={past().length === 0}
      onPress={undo}
    />
    <Button
      variant="ghost"
      icon={Redo2}
      accessibilityLabel="Redo"
      disabled={future().length === 0}
      onPress={redo}
    />
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator style={toolbarRule()} />
  <Menu>
    <MenuTrigger>
      <View
        role="button"
        accessibilityLabel={`Block: ${doc().block}`}
        accessibilityState={{ expanded: open() }}
        {...toggleLook({ on: open, text: true })}
      >
        <Text style={toggleLabel(open)}>{doc().block}</Text>
        <Text style={toggleLabel(open)}>▾</Text>
      </View>
    </MenuTrigger>
    <MenuContent>
      {BLOCKS.map((block) => (
        <MenuRadioItem checked={doc().block === block} onSelect={() => commit({ block })}>
          {block}
        </MenuRadioItem>
      ))}
    </MenuContent>
  </Menu>
  <ToolbarSeparator style={toolbarRule()} />
  <ToggleGroup inset={false}>
    {MARKS.map((mark) => (
      <Toggle
        pressed={doc().marks.includes(mark)}
        accessibilityLabel={mark}
        onChange={({ pressed }) => commit({ marks: withMark(mark, pressed) })}
      >
        {mark}
      </Toggle>
    ))}
  </ToggleGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator style={toolbarRule()} />
  <ToolbarGroup accessibilityLabel="Alignment" style={{ gap: 2 }}>
    {ALIGNS.map((align) => (
      <Toggle
        pressed={doc().align === align}
        accessibilityLabel={align}
        onChange={({ pressed }) => {
          if (pressed) commit({ align });
        }}
      >
        {align}
      </Toggle>
    ))}
  </ToolbarGroup>
</Toolbar>;
```

### Overflow [#overflow]

Add `ToolbarOverflow` and wrap foldable tools in `ToolbarButton` so the bar measures each item with
`onLayout` and folds lower-priority tools into the `"⋯"` menu as the bar narrows. Give a
`ToolbarGroup` `fold="unit"` (the default) to fold the whole group together under its
`accessibilityLabel`, or `fold="none"` to let its `ToolbarButton`s fold individually by their own
`priority`. The bar draws the hairline rules between visible units and hides until its initial
measurements arrive.

```tsx
import { MenuCheckboxItem, MenuItem, MenuRadioItem } from "@/components/ui/menu";
import { Toolbar, ToolbarGroup, ToolbarButton, ToolbarOverflow } from "@/components/ui/toolbar";

<Toolbar accessibilityLabel="Formatting" style={{ alignSelf: "stretch" }}>
  <ToolbarGroup accessibilityLabel="History" fold="none">
    <ToolbarButton
      priority={4}
      menu={
        <MenuItem disabled={past().length === 0} onSelect={undo}>
          Undo
        </MenuItem>
      }
    >
      <Button
        variant="ghost"
        icon={Undo2}
        accessibilityLabel="Undo"
        disabled={past().length === 0}
        onPress={undo}
      />
    </ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton
      priority={3}
      menu={
        <MenuItem disabled={future().length === 0} onSelect={redo}>
          Redo
        </MenuItem>
      }
    >
      <Button
        variant="ghost"
        icon={Redo2}
        accessibilityLabel="Redo"
        disabled={future().length === 0}
        onPress={redo}
      />
    </ToolbarButton>
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarGroup accessibilityLabel="Marks" fold="none">
    {MARKS.map((mark) => (
      <ToolbarButton
        foldable={mark !== "bold"}
        priority={mark === "italic" ? 5 : 1}
        menu={
          <MenuCheckboxItem checked={has(mark)} onSelect={() => toggle(mark)}>
            {mark}
          </MenuCheckboxItem>
        }
      >
        <Toggle pressed={has(mark)} accessibilityLabel={mark} onChange={() => toggle(mark)}>
          {mark}
        </Toggle>
      </ToolbarButton>
    ))}
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarGroup accessibilityLabel="Alignment" priority={2} fold="unit">
    {ALIGNS.map((align) => (
      <ToolbarButton
        menu={
          <MenuRadioItem checked={doc().align === align} onSelect={() => setAlign(align)}>
            {align}
          </MenuRadioItem>
        }
      >
        <Toggle
          pressed={doc().align === align}
          accessibilityLabel={align}
          onChange={() => setAlign(align)}
        >
          {align}
        </Toggle>
      </ToolbarButton>
    ))}
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarOverflow accessibilityLabel="More formatting">
    <MenuItem onSelect={clear}>Clear formatting</MenuItem>
  </ToolbarOverflow>
</Toolbar>;
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh/base` Toolbar](https://nsh.dev/elements/toolbar), `ToolbarGroup` and `ToolbarSeparator` passes through. `style` goes over the look's. Items keep their own look (`Button`, `Toggle`, …).

| Part               | Props                                                                                                                                         | Description                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Toolbar`          | `axis`, and every `nsh/base` Toolbar prop                                                                                                     | The bar: one toolbar for screen readers, arrow keys along `axis`, on the track                                                                 |
| `ToolbarGroup`     | `priority`, `fold` (`"unit" \| "none"`), and every `nsh/base` ToolbarGroup prop                                                               | A named run of items; its direction follows the bar, and with `ToolbarOverflow` it folds as one unit or per item                               |
| `ToolbarSeparator` | every `nsh/base` ToolbarSeparator prop                                                                                                        | The hairline between runs, never a tab stop (omitted when `ToolbarOverflow` manages the rules between visible units)                           |
| `ToolbarButton`    | `menu`, `priority`, `foldable`, `class`, `style`                                                                                              | Wraps one tool so a bar with `ToolbarOverflow` can measure its width and fold it into `"⋯"` when space runs out                                |
| `ToolbarOverflow`  | `accessibilityLabel`, `label`, `open`, `defaultOpen`, `onOpenChange`, `tooltip`, `disabled`, `align`, `offset`, `margin`, `style`, `children` | The `"⋯"` trigger and menu showing folded tools in bar order (grouped under each `ToolbarGroup`'s `accessibilityLabel`), before any `children` |

A bar without `ToolbarOverflow` behaves identically to a static bar. In a bar with `ToolbarOverflow`
on a horizontal non-terminal surface, unmeasured items stay visible rather than blocking folding.
Because `nsh/base`'s `Button`, `Toggle` and `Link` do not forward `onFocus`/`onBlur`, `Toolbar` does
not expose `onFocusIn`/`onFocusOut`, and `nsh/base`'s roving focus marks non-stop items
`focusable={false}` (`roving.rs`), focus cannot automatically move to `"⋯"` when a focused tool
folds while an earlier tool remains visible.

`toolbarTrack({ vertical })` (`@/lib/ui/tool`) and `toolbarRule(vertical)` are the look, for a bar of your own.

# Tooltip (/dev/docs/components/tooltip)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add tooltip
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Tooltip, TooltipContent, TooltipTrigger } from "@/components/ui/tooltip";
import { Icon } from "@/lib/ui/icons";
```

The examples draw icons with `Icon` from `lib/ui/icons`; see [Icons](../icons) for adding it and picking a size and color.

```tsx
<Tooltip>
  <TooltipTrigger>Add to favorites</TooltipTrigger>
  <TooltipContent>Add to favorites</TooltipContent>
</Tooltip>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Tooltip`:

```text
Tooltip
├── TooltipTrigger
└── TooltipContent
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Placement [#placement]

```tsx
<Tooltip placement="top">…</Tooltip>
<Tooltip placement="bottom">…</Tooltip>
```

### Rich [#rich]

A title and a note in a column, 10 points of padding.

```tsx
<TooltipContent rich>
  <Text class={tooltipText}>Delete forever</Text>
  <Text style={tooltipNote()}>⌘⌫</Text>
</TooltipContent>
```

### On any element's `tooltip` prop [#on-any-elements-tooltip-prop]

`nsh/base` takes a hint as a host's `tooltip`; `TooltipContent` alone is that hint.

```tsx
<Button tooltip={<TooltipContent>Add to favorites</TooltipContent>}>Star</Button>
```

### A trigger of your own [#a-trigger-of-your-own]

A string child is a `Button`; anything else is the element itself, and its own press, hover
and name stay.

```tsx
<TooltipTrigger variant="ghost">Star</TooltipTrigger>
<TooltipTrigger>
  <Icon icon={Star} size={16} tint={colors.mutedForeground} />
</TooltipTrigger>
```

### On a menu's trigger [#on-a-menus-trigger]

A tooltip hangs on the element the trigger is. Give that element the `tooltip` prop and
hand it to the trigger that wants the press; do not nest `TooltipTrigger` around a trigger
part, which draws nothing for the hint's host to wrap.

```tsx
<Menu>
  <MenuTrigger>
    <View
      accessibilityLabel="More actions"
      tooltip={<TooltipContent>More actions</TooltipContent>}
      style={{ width: 28, height: 28, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}
    >
      <Icon icon={Ellipsis} size={16} tint={colors.mutedForeground} />
    </View>
  </MenuTrigger>
  <MenuContent>…</MenuContent>
</Menu>
```

## API [#api]

`nsh/base`'s Tooltip is the bubble itself, shown through a host's `tooltip` prop, so the root renders one host view around its trigger. `TooltipContent` mounts [`nsh/base` Tooltip](https://nsh.dev/elements/tooltip); every base prop passes through and `class` goes over `tooltipLook`'s.

| Part                                          | Props                                                                                                                               | Description                                                                            |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Tooltip`                                     | `open` / `defaultOpen`, `placement`, `align`, `offset`, `margin`, `delay`, `disabled`, `style`, `onOpenChange`, `onOpen`, `onClose` | The root: it owns whether the hint shows, and renders one host view around its trigger |
| `TooltipTrigger`                              | The host: `variant` (a string child's `Button`), `disabled`, `style`                                                                | The element the hint hangs on                                                          |
| `TooltipContent`                              | The bubble: `rich`, and base's `placement`, `align`, `offset`, `margin`, `delay`, `disabled`; alone, it is a host's `tooltip`       | The hint itself, in the look of `tooltipLook`                                          |
| `tooltipLook`, `tooltipText`, `tooltipNote()` | `rich`                                                                                                                              | The look's parts, for a bubble of your own                                             |

# Trace (/dev/docs/components/trace)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add trace
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import {
  Trace,
  TraceCollapsible,
  TraceCollapsibleContent,
  TraceCollapsibleTrigger,
  TraceDescription,
  TraceIcon,
  TraceLine,
  TraceTitle,
} from "@/components/ui/trace";
```

```tsx
<Trace>
  <TraceLine status="running">
    <TraceIcon>
      <Icon icon={Globe} size={16} tint={colors.mutedForeground} />
    </TraceIcon>
    <TraceTitle>Searching the web</TraceTitle>
  </TraceLine>
</Trace>
```

## Composition [#composition]

Use the following composition to build a `Trace`:

```text
Trace
├── TraceLine
│   ├── TraceIcon
│   ├── TraceTitle
│   └── TraceDescription
└── TraceCollapsible
    ├── TraceCollapsibleTrigger
    │   └── TraceLine
    └── TraceCollapsibleContent
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Reasoning [#reasoning]

A reasoning line counts while the model thinks (`status="running"`: a `Spinner` in the icon slot, the title pulsing) and then reads what it took. The pulse stands still when the user asks for less motion. It opens onto the text. `open` with `onOpenChange` lets the app open it when the thought is done.

```tsx
<Trace>
  <TraceCollapsible open={open()} onOpenChange={(event) => open.set(event.open)}>
    <TraceCollapsibleTrigger>
      <TraceLine status={thinking() ? "running" : undefined}>
        <TraceIcon>
          <Icon icon={Brain} size={16} tint={colors.mutedForeground} />
        </TraceIcon>
        <TraceTitle>{thinking() ? "Thinking…" : "Thought for"}</TraceTitle>
        <TraceDescription>{seconds()} s</TraceDescription>
      </TraceLine>
    </TraceCollapsibleTrigger>
    <TraceCollapsibleContent>{thought}</TraceCollapsibleContent>
  </TraceCollapsible>
</Trace>
```

### A tool call [#a-tool-call]

A call goes `pending` (dimmed), `running`, then done (no status), and opens onto what it did. The result is a [`CodeBlock`](./code-block): a search, a weather lookup and a code run are the same `Trace` with a different body — a list of [`Item`](./item)s, a card, a `CodeBlock` — not a card of their own. Disable the trigger until there is something to show.

```tsx
<TraceCollapsible open={open()} onOpenChange={(event) => open.set(event.open)}>
  <TraceCollapsibleTrigger disabled={call.state !== "done"}>
    <TraceLine
      status={
        call.state === "queued" ? "pending" : call.state === "running" ? "running" : undefined
      }
    >
      <TraceIcon>
        <Icon icon={Terminal} size={16} tint={colors.mutedForeground} />
      </TraceIcon>
      <TraceTitle>Run code</TraceTitle>
      <TraceDescription>{call.note}</TraceDescription>
    </TraceLine>
  </TraceCollapsibleTrigger>
  <TraceCollapsibleContent>
    <CodeBlock size="sm">
      <CodeBlockContent>{call.code}</CodeBlockContent>
    </CodeBlock>
  </TraceCollapsibleContent>
</TraceCollapsible>
```

### Sources [#sources]

A `TraceLine` with `onPress` is a pressable: it takes the text color under the pointer and the focus ring with the keyboard on it. Use it for a source that opens a page.

```tsx
<Trace>
  <TraceLine onPress={() => openUrl(source.url)}>
    <TraceIcon>
      <Icon icon={FileText} size={16} tint={colors.mutedForeground} />
    </TraceIcon>
    <TraceTitle>{source.title}</TraceTitle>
    <TraceDescription>{source.site}</TraceDescription>
  </TraceLine>
</Trace>
```

### A failed step [#a-failed-step]

`status="error"` takes the destructive role for the title and the chevron; tint the icon with `colors.destructive` yourself, since an `Icon` draws in the tint it is given. A failed call opens onto its log in a destructive `CodeBlock`.

```tsx
<TraceCollapsible defaultOpen>
  <TraceCollapsibleTrigger>
    <TraceLine status="error">
      <TraceIcon>
        <Icon icon={CircleAlert} size={16} tint={colors.destructive} />
      </TraceIcon>
      <TraceTitle>Run code failed</TraceTitle>
      <TraceDescription>exit 1</TraceDescription>
    </TraceLine>
  </TraceCollapsibleTrigger>
  <TraceCollapsibleContent>
    <CodeBlock size="sm" variant="destructive">
      <CodeBlockContent wrap>{log}</CodeBlockContent>
    </CodeBlock>
  </TraceCollapsibleContent>
</TraceCollapsible>
```

## API [#api]

Every prop of [`nsh` View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view) passes through on every part but `TraceTitle` and `TraceDescription` (a [`nsh` Text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text)), `TraceCollapsible` (the props below) and `TraceCollapsibleContent` (`nsh/base`'s Collapsible); `style` goes over the look's.

| Part                      | Props                                                                                              | Description                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Trace`                   | —                                                                                                  | The column of steps.                                                                                            |
| `TraceLine`               | `status`: `"running" \| "pending" \| "error"` (default none: done); `onPress`: `() => void`        | One step. With `onPress` it is a pressable. `running` pulses the title, `pending` dims, `error` is destructive. |
| `TraceIcon`               | —                                                                                                  | The icon slot, the theme's middle icon square; a `Spinner` while the line is `running`.                         |
| `TraceTitle`              | —                                                                                                  | What the step is doing or did: one line, cut with an ellipsis.                                                  |
| `TraceDescription`        | —                                                                                                  | A quieter note: a duration, a count; digits do not jump.                                                        |
| `TraceCollapsible`        | `open`: `boolean`; `defaultOpen`: `boolean`; `onOpenChange`: `(event: { open, reason }) => void`   | A line and what it opens onto; owns whether it is open.                                                         |
| `TraceCollapsibleTrigger` | `disabled`: `boolean`; `accessibilityLabel`; `style`, `hoverStyle`, `focusVisibleStyle`            | The pressable row: a `TraceLine` and a chevron that turns a quarter as it opens.                                |
| `TraceCollapsibleContent` | `children`: `string \| JSX.Element` (a string is muted text); `reveal`: `boolean` (default `true`) | The panel under the line.                                                                                       |

`traceLook()` is exported for a trace the app draws itself: its parts as the styles they wear (`root`, `line`, `icon`, `title`, `description`, `collapsible`, `trigger`, `chevron`, `content`).

# Tree (/dev/docs/components/tree)

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add tree
```

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Tree } from "@/components/ui/tree";
```

```tsx
<Tree items={items} defaultExpanded={["src"]} />
```

## Examples [#examples]

### Folders [#folders]

`items` nest; a folder opens with a press or its chevron.

```tsx
const items: TreeItem[] = [
  {
    id: "src",
    label: "src",
    children: [
      { id: "app", label: "App.tsx" },
      { id: "kit", label: "kit.tsx" },
    ],
  },
  { id: "readme", label: "README.md" },
];

<Tree items={items} style={{ width: 280, maxHeight: 220 }} />;
```

### Expanded [#expanded]

`defaultExpanded` opens folders at first.

```tsx
<Tree items={items} defaultExpanded={["src"]} />
```

### Height [#height]

A row is `treeRowHeight` tall: 28 points with a pointer, 44 on a touch screen. A well that should be
as tall as its first rows, with the rest scrolling, sets its own height from it (`Tree`'s `style`),
plus the list's 6 points of padding on each side.

```tsx
import { treeRowHeight } from "@/components/ui/tree";

<Tree items={items} style={{ height: 8 * treeRowHeight + 12 }} />;
```

### A large tree [#a-large-tree]

A hundred folders of a hundred files: 10 100 items. The tree is virtualized, so only the rows in view are made; opening a folder adds its hundred rows without a stall. Give it a height (the tree scrolls inside it) and keep `expanded` and `selected` as signals if you read them.

```tsx
const logs: TreeItem[] = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, f) => ({
  id: `f${f}`,
  label: `Folder ${String(f + 1).padStart(3, "0")}`,
  children: Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) => ({
    id: `f${f}/${i}`,
    label: `file-${f + 1}-${i + 1}.log`,
  })),
}));

<Tree
  items={logs}
  expanded={open()}
  selected={selected()}
  accessibilityLabel="Logs"
  style={{ height: 288 }}
  onExpandedChange={({ expanded }) => open.set(expanded)}
  onSelectedChange={({ selected }) => selected.set(selected)}
/>;
```

## API [#api]

Uses `treeItemClass` and `TreeRow` by default. Every prop of [`nsh/base` Tree](https://nsh.dev/elements/tree) passes through.

| Part            | Props                                                                                | Description                                                     |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Tree`          | `items`, `defaultExpanded`, `renderItem`, `onSelect`, and every `nsh/base` Tree prop | The virtualized list of rows, in a card, `TreeRow` by default   |
| `TreeRow`       | `entry`, `icon`, `tint`, `detail`                                                    | A row: its chevron, its icon, its label and a detail at the end |
| `treeItemClass` | —                                                                                    | The row's look, for a row you draw yourself                     |
| `treeRowHeight` | —                                                                                    | A row's height: 28 with a pointer, 44 on a touch screen         |

# Components (/dev/docs/components)

83 components, one page each: Installation, Usage, an optional Composition,
Examples and API. They are grouped in two: <strong>Base</strong>, aligned with an NSH element,
and <strong>Enhanced</strong>, this library's additions with no NSH element of their own.
Behavior, keyboard support and the full unstyled props live on
[nsh.dev/elements](https://nsh.dev/elements); each page links its base element and the shadcn/ui
component it stands in for.

The list is generated from `registry.json` and these pages, so every `registry:ui` item has a page
and every page has an item. The group comes from 

<a href="/docs/components/coverage">Coverage</a>: a page registered in one of its NSH rows is
Base, one in none is Enhanced. Add one with `npx shadcn-nsh@latest add <name>`.

<ComponentsIndex kind="official" />

## Enhanced [#enhanced]
