# Customizing (/dev/docs/customizing)

`init` and `add` copy files into the app; after that they are the app's own. There are three places to change them.

| Change                 | Where                                                    | Reaches                                   |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Colors, radii, shadows | `theme.json`, `lib/ui/semantics.json`                    | every component                           |
| One control's look     | its `*Look` function in `components/ui/<id>.tsx`         | that control's variants, sizes and states |
| Structure or API       | the component and parts after the look, in the same file | that component's props and parts          |

In a monorepo, every path starts at `packages/ui/` instead of the app root.

## Colors, radii and shadows [#colors-radii-and-shadows]

`theme.json` holds the colors for both appearances, the three `radius-*` layer lengths, and font families; `lib/ui/semantics.json` holds style groups and surface finishes (`shared` + sparse `light`/`dark`), referencing tokens with `{token}`. Every component reads them through `lib/ui/theme.ts`.

```sh
theme.json               # base tokens: colors, 3 radii, fonts
lib/ui/semantics.json    # style groups and surface finishes
lib/ui/theme.ts          # colors, finish, shape, font, control, focusRing, alpha
```

Edit the values and keep the keys: components and finishes refer to them by name, and both appearances need the same merged finish shape. This is the change that reaches every component at once. [Theme](./theme) lists the roles.

A copied `semantics.json` writes every field of every finish, so nothing here is guessed: a field the theme does not care about carries its neutral value — `material: null`, `backdropFilter: "none"`, `elevation: null`, `gradient: null` (a flat fill), the pressed pair `null` (pressing only dims), and no colour of its own on the top or bottom edge, which then takes the finish's `border-color`. In the library's own sources those neutrals are written once in `packages/theme/tokens/base/style.shared.tokens.json`; in a copied app they are simply there. If you add a finish role, copy every field of a neighbouring role and change the ones that differ, and state device-dependent sizes twice, under `pointer` and `touch`, with the same keys.

```json
{
  "cssVars": {
    "theme": {
      "radius": "8px",
      "radius-control": "8px",
      "radius-container": "12px",
      "radius-modal": "14px"
    },
    "light": { "background": "#f6f6f9", "primary": "#c6ef6a" },
    "dark": { "background": "#16191f", "primary": "#c4ec6a" }
  }
}
```

## One control's look [#one-controls-look]

The look is the function that turns a `variant` (shadcn's word: `default`, `secondary`, `ghost`, `destructive`), a `size` (`sm`, `default`, `lg`), a `tone` (the theme's `Tone`: `neutral`, `accent`, `info`, `warn`, `destructive`, `up`, `down`) and a state into the props `nsh/base` draws with. It sits at the top of a copied component, above the component itself.

```tsx
// components/ui/button.tsx
export function buttonLook(variant: Live<ButtonVariant> = "secondary", o?: ButtonLookOptions) {
  return {
    get style(): ViewStyle {
      const dims = dimensions(o);
      return {
        height: terminal ? TERMINAL_ROW : dims.height,
        borderRadius: shape.control,
        // ...
      };
    },
    // hoverStyle, activeStyle, focusVisibleStyle, disabledStyle, hitSlop
  };
}
```

Change the values in that function — a height, a radius, a hover fill — and the shell below still spreads the result. Keep the props it returns; they are what the base control reads. `buttonLook` is one; `iconButtonLook`, `roundButtonLook` and `splitButtonLook` live in the same file, and other components name theirs the same way (`switchLook`, `checkboxLook`). Controls whose shape and dimensions vary by platform (`checkbox`, `switch`, `slider`, `radio-group`, `progress`, `spinner`, `calendar`, `sheet`, and shared `lib/indicator.ts` for fields) read the four control dimensions the theme states through `control()`; the per-component geometry that hangs off them stays right inside those component or lib files.

## Structure and API [#structure-and-api]

The shell is the component and its parts, below the look. It reads props, spreads the look and gives a composite its roles.

```tsx
// components/ui/button.tsx
export function Button(props: ButtonProps) { ... }
export function IconButton(props: IconButtonProps) { ... }
```

```tsx
// components/ui/dialog.tsx
export function Dialog(props: DialogProps) { ... }
export function DialogTrigger(props: DialogTriggerProps) { ... }
export function DialogContent(props: DialogContentProps) { ... }
```

Change the shell to change which props a component takes, which parts it exports, and how they nest. A new prop is read in the shell and passed to the base control; keep the caller's `style`, `hoverStyle` and other style props after the look's, so they still win. Behavior — keyboard, focus, dismissal — stays in `nsh/base`; the shell passes its props through. See [nsh.dev/elements](https://nsh.dev/elements).

## After an update [#after-an-update]

`add` keeps a file the app changed and reports it; `diff` shows the lines; `add --overwrite` replaces it. `theme.json` and `semantics.json` are the exceptions: one with missing keys is merged, and customized values are kept unless `--overwrite`.

# Getting started (/dev/docs/getting-started)

## An existing NSH app [#an-existing-nsh-app]

An app with `nsh.json` (from `nsh init`) is ready:

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest init
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button
```

`init` writes `nsh-ui.json`, installs the theme and points each `nsh.json` at `theme.json`; in an app it also sets up the `@/` import alias the docs' snippets use — `"@/*": ["./*"]` in `tsconfig.json`'s `compilerOptions.paths` (writing the file when there is none) and `"resolve": { "alias": { "@": "./" } }` in `nsh.json` — leaving values already there alone with a warning. `add` copies the component and its `registryDependencies` (the theme and the shared look files it imports) into the app; from then on the files are the app's own. [CLI](./cli) has every command, flag and default.

Consumer monorepo scaffolding (`shadcn-nsh create`) is not built. `init` and `add` work in a workspace that already has `apps/*` and a `packages/ui` named `@workspace/ui` (or already holding `nsh-ui.json`).

## Commands [#commands]

| Command           | What it does                                                                                 |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `init`            | Writes `nsh-ui.json`, installs a theme, points each `nsh.json` at it, sets up `@/` in an app |
| `add [items…]`    | Copies items and their `registryDependencies` into the app                                   |
| `list`            | The registry's items, `✓` on the ones the app has                                            |
| `view <items…>`   | The files `add` would write: target paths and contents                                       |
| `diff [items…]`   | The app's files against the registry's; exits 1 when they differ                             |
| `build` / `serve` | Build `registry.json` into `public/r`, or serve it locally                                   |

Every command takes `-c, --cwd <dir>` (default: the current directory). `init`, `add`, `list`, `view` and `diff` also take `--registry <url>`, a template with `{name}` in it. [CLI](./cli) has every flag and default.

## Add [#add]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button -c apps/web
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add --all
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button --dry-run
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button --overwrite
```

- A file the app does not have is written; one identical to the registry's is skipped.
- A file the app changed is kept and reported: `kept components/ui/button.tsx, differs (run diff)`. `--overwrite` replaces it and prints the change: `overwrite components/ui/button.tsx (+2 -1)`.
- `theme.json` and `lib/ui/semantics.json` are merged by key: the app keeps its colors and semantic values and gains any tokens, style keys, or finishes it lacks. Customized theme files stay as they are.
- `--all` adds every `registry:ui` item, dependencies included.
- `--dry-run` writes nothing — not even `nsh-ui.json` or the theme — and prints what it would write.

## list, view, diff [#list-view-diff]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest list
npx shadcn-nsh@latest view button
npx shadcn-nsh@latest diff
npx shadcn-nsh@latest diff button
```

`list` reads the catalog (`index.json`) and marks an item when any of its files is in the app; `--json` prints the same catalog for tooling. `view` prints what `add` would write, dependencies first, with imports rewritten for the app. `diff` compares the same rewritten content with the app's files; without an item it lists the installed items that differ, with one it prints the changed lines, and it exits 1 when anything differs:

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest diff || echo "run shadcn-nsh add <item> --overwrite"
```

## Monorepo [#monorepo]

If the workspace has `apps/web` and a `packages/ui` named `@workspace/ui`:

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add button -c apps/web
```

The files install into `packages/ui`, and the app imports them through the workspace:

```tsx
import { Button } from "@workspace/ui/components/ui/button";
```

## Local registry [#local-registry]

When developing this repository:

```sh
bun run registry:build
bun run registry:serve
bun run shadcn-nsh -- add button -c apps/web --registry "http://127.0.0.1:4173/{name}.json"
```

## Theme [#theme]

The look is `theme.json` (base tokens: colors, three `radius-*` layer lengths, and fonts) and `lib/ui/semantics.json` (cross-platform semantics: style groups and `shared` + sparse `light`/`dark` finishes); `lib/ui/theme.ts` reads both. `init` installs them and points each `nsh.json` at `theme.json`; in a monorepo they live under `packages/ui`. See [Theme](./theme) for the keys, and [Customizing](./customizing) to change colors, one control's look, or its shell after copying.

## Behavior, previews and native tests [#behavior-previews-and-native-tests]

| Surface        | Role                                                             |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `apps/website` | Public docs; `apps/website/demos/<id>.tsx` is the page's preview |
| `apps/gallery` | Native behavior tests and smoke pages for the same components    |

Behavior, keyboard support and accessibility belong to `nsh/base`: [nsh.dev/elements](https://nsh.dev/elements). This site documents install, usage, examples and the props the styled layer adds.

# Icons (/dev/docs/icons)

The icons are [lucide](https://lucide.dev/icons)'s, drawn by `Icon` from `lib/ui/icons.tsx`: an icon is a lucide node, stroked on a canvas in its 24-unit box, so it reads at the same size and weight as lucide anywhere else.

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add icons
```

This copies `lib/ui/icons.tsx` and `lib/icon-drawing.ts` (the drawing and the image form, apart from NSH so a unit test reads them) and installs `lucide`. A component that draws icons of its own (`select`, `menu`, `tabs`, `sidebar`…) brings them when it is added. `button`, `alert`, `empty` and the other components that take an icon as a child do not: add `icons` once before writing the examples on their pages.

## Usage [#usage]

```tsx
import { Plus } from "lucide";

import { Icon } from "@/lib/ui/icons";
import { colors } from "@/lib/ui/theme";
```

```tsx
<Icon icon={Plus} size={16} tint={colors.foreground} />
```

Import each icon by name from `lucide`, as a front end does: the [icon list](https://lucide.dev/icons) gives the names (`ChevronDown`, `Trash`, `CircleX`). The color is one of the theme's roles, never a literal.

## Size and color [#size-and-color]

Inside a component, the component says how large an icon is and what color it takes, so it matches the label beside it in every variant and state. Spread its glyph helper, or use its size constant:

```tsx
import { RotateCw, Trash } from "lucide";

import { Button, buttonGlyph, IconButton, iconButtonGlyph } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Icon } from "@/lib/ui/icons";

<Button accessibilityLabel="Retry the upload" onPress={retry}>
  <Icon icon={RotateCw} {...buttonGlyph("secondary")} />
</Button>

<IconButton variant="destructive" accessibilityLabel="Delete" onPress={remove}>
  <Icon icon={Trash} {...iconButtonGlyph({ variant: "destructive" })} />
</IconButton>
```

| Component    | Helper                                                                  |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `button`     | `buttonGlyph`, `iconButtonGlyph`, `roundButtonGlyph`                    |
| `toggle`     | `toggleGlyph`                                                           |
| `menu`       | `menuItemGlyph`                                                         |
| `attachment` | `attachmentGlyph`                                                       |
| `alert`      | `ALERT_ICON` (the size; the color is `colors.foreground` or the tone's) |
| `empty`      | `EMPTY_ICON`                                                            |

A part that takes an icon as a prop, such as `SelectTrigger`'s `icon` or `MarkerIcon`'s, takes the lucide node itself (`icon={Calendar}`) and draws it in its own size and color.

## In a native menu [#in-a-native-menu]

A native menu draws its own items, so it takes an image rather than a view: an item's `icon` is what `<Image>`'s `src` takes, fitted to the menu's icon size. `iconImage` writes a lucide node as that image, stroked in `currentColor`, so the menu draws it in its own text color:

```tsx
import { Copy, Mail, Share2 } from "lucide";
import { Menu } from "nsh/desktop";

import { iconImage } from "@/lib/ui/icons";

const shareMenu = () =>
  Menu.popup([
    { label: "Copy", icon: iconImage(Copy), onSelect: copy },
    {
      label: "Share",
      icon: iconImage(Share2),
      submenu: [{ label: "Mail", icon: iconImage(Mail), onSelect: mail }],
    },
  ]);
```

The application menu's items take it the same way (`Menu.setApplicationMenu`). `iconImage(icon, options?)`:

| Argument         | Type       | Default          | Description                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `icon`           | `IconNode` |                  | The icon, as `lucide` exports it.                                                                                                 |
| `options.weight` | `number`   | `2`              | The stroke in the 24-unit box (lucide's own is 2).                                                                                |
| `options.ink`    | `string`   | `"currentColor"` | The stroke's color. A fixed ink makes the image a template image, which `tintColor` recolors instead (`CheckMark` passes `#000`). |

## Props [#props]

| Prop     | Type       | Default | Description                                             |
| -------- | ---------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `icon`   | `IconNode` |         | The icon, as `lucide` exports it.                       |
| `size`   | `number`   | `20`    | The side of its square, in points.                      |
| `tint`   | `string`   |         | The stroke color, and the fill with `fill`.             |
| `weight` | `number`   | `2`     | The stroke in the 24-unit box (lucide's own is 2).      |
| `fill`   | `boolean`  | `false` | Fill the shape instead of stroking it (a solid `Play`). |

The arrows and chevrons that point along the line (`ChevronLeft`, `ChevronRight`, `ArrowLeft`, `ArrowRight`) are mirrored in a right-to-left layout.

## In the terminal [#in-the-terminal]

The terminal draws no icons: `Icon` shows nothing there, except `Check`, which is the mark `✓`. An icon-only control uses `IconLabel` instead, which shows a short word in the icon's place:

```tsx
import { IconLabel } from "@/lib/ui/icons";

<IconButton accessibilityLabel="Close" onPress={close}>
  <IconLabel icon={X} label="close" {...iconButtonGlyph()} />
</IconButton>;
```

## Changing them [#changing-them]

`lib/ui/icons.tsx` is the app's own after `add`. To use another set, keep `Icon`'s props and change what it draws: the components only ever pass an icon, a size, a tint and a weight.

# Theme (/dev/docs/theme)

The theme is the upstream gallery's: a graphite page (paper in light appearance), cards and insets, one citrus accent, compact controls with a pointer and roomier ones on a touch screen. It is two JSON files — base tokens in `theme.json` and cross-platform semantics in `semantics.json`, following the [design-semantics standard](https://github.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/blob/main/docs/specs/design-semantics.md) — plus the module that reads them, and every component takes its colors, radii, typography, motion and depth from there. No component writes a color of its own.

## Files [#files]

| File                                    | What it holds                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `theme.json`                            | Base tokens: colors (light / dark and shared), the three `radius-*` layer lengths (plus `radius`), in shadcn's `cssVars` shape                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `light.tokens.json`, `dark.tokens.json` | Standalone W3C DTCG 2025.10 Format files resolved per appearance at the `pointer` tier (in-file aliases, 6-digit `hex` fallbacks) for Figma Variables (Light/Dark modes), Tokens Studio, and Style Dictionary v4; static snapshots as shipped                                                                                                                             |
| `DESIGN.md`                             | Generated Google Labs DESIGN.md (`alpha`) specification for coding agents, compiled from DTCG sources and the pointer-tier `light`/`dark` resolutions; static snapshot as shipped                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `semantics.json`                        | Semantic layer in DTCG names: 7 style groups (`typography`, `dimension` — with the four control dimensions under `dimension.control` — `shape`, `state`, `transition`, `motion` (three timings plus the `state` fade), `controls`), `elevation` (the shadow scale, per appearance) and `finishes` (`shared` + sparse `light` / `dark`), referencing tokens with `{token}` |
| `lib/ui/theme.ts`                       | `colors`, `finish`, `shape`, `font`, `style`, `control`, `focusRing` and `alpha`, read reactively from `theme.json` and `semantics.json`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

## Installation [#installation]

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest add theme
```

`add theme` writes `theme.json`, `light.tokens.json`, `dark.tokens.json`, `DESIGN.md`, `lib/ui/semantics.json` and `lib/ui/theme.ts`, the data of the theme `nsh-ui.json` records (`theme-shadcn` writes shadcn's into `themes/shadcn/`). `init` writes the same files and also points each `nsh.json` at `theme.json`. In a monorepo they live under `packages/ui`. Every component depends on it.

`light.tokens.json`, `dark.tokens.json` and `DESIGN.md` are generated outputs: import `.tokens.json` into Figma Variables as Light and Dark modes, Tokens Studio, or Style Dictionary v4, and let coding agents read `DESIGN.md` for the theme's tokens and design rationale. Because they describe the theme as shipped, editing `theme.json` or `semantics.json` later does not update them.

## Colors [#colors]

`theme.json` is a shadcn theme: `cssVars.theme` holds the radii and the accent's raw values, `cssVars.light` and `cssVars.dark` hold the same semantic keys for the two appearances. The core keys are shadcn's (`background`, `foreground`, `card`, `popover`, `primary`, `secondary`, `muted`, `accent`, `destructive`, `border`, `input`, `ring`, `chart-1` … `chart-5`, `sidebar*`). Upstream adds the roles the gallery needs:

| Role                                                                  | Use                                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `inset` / `raised`                                                    | A surface inside a card, and a control on the card                                                          |
| `field` / `input`                                                     | An input's well and its edge                                                                                |
| `line` / `border`                                                     | Hairlines inside insets, and the edge of a card or control                                                  |
| `hover` / `faint`                                                     | The pointer's wash, and the quietest text                                                                   |
| `brand`                                                               | The accent as ink                                                                                           |
| `track` / `knob`                                                      | A switch's track when off, and a switch's knob; sliders and progress bars read their preset's track role    |
| `info` / `warn` / `up`                                                | The tones beside the accent; a data loss reads `destructive`                                                |
| `brand-tint`, `info-tint`, `warn-tint`, `destructive-tint`, `up-tint` | The same tones as fills behind text (negative trend reuses `destructive-tint`)                              |
| `inverse` / `inverse-foreground` / `inverse-brand`                    | A toast's and a tooltip's reversed surface, its text and action; quieter ink is `finish.inverse.foreground` |

`colors` maps the roles a component names onto those keys:

```tsx
import { colors } from "@shadcn-nsh/theme";

colors.background; // the page
colors.card; // a card
colors.inset; // a surface inside a card
colors.raised; // a control on a card
colors.field; // an input's well
colors.foreground; // body text
colors.mutedForeground; // secondary text
colors.brand; // the accent as ink
colors.primary; // the accent as a fill
colors.primaryForeground; // what reads on that fill
colors.destructive; // a failure
colors.up; // additions
```

Read a role where it is drawn (in JSX, a `draw`, or an effect): the getters read the token then, so they follow the appearance.

## Finishes [#finishes]

A finish is light and depth: what a surface is filled with, and how it sits above what is behind it. There are fourteen — eleven layers a component can be drawn on, and three states — and a finish states the same fields in every theme: `background`, `foreground`, `shadow`, `material`, `gradient`, `backdropFilter`, the three border colours, the pressed pair and `elevation`. A field a theme leaves out is not missing — it takes a neutral value, written once in the base token set (`tokens/base/style.shared.tokens.json`) and compiled into every theme's `semantics.json`: `material: null` (no platform material), `backdropFilter: "none"`, `elevation: null`, `gradient: null` (flat), no colour of its own on the top or bottom edge, and the pressed pair `null` (pressing only dims). In the DTCG sources those neutrals are written `"none"` in the finish group's `$extensions`, since a token's `$value` cannot be `null`; a token a theme writes wins over it. `semantics.json` keeps `finishes.shared` (fields identical in both appearances, referencing `{token}` so NSH's `token()` handles light/dark switching) plus sparse `finishes.light` and `finishes.dark` overrides, and `finish.<role>` merges them and resolves every `{token}` (including `oklch(from {card} l c h / 0.78)`) for the active appearance.

| Role       | Use                                                                |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `card`     | A surface that holds content: a card, a section                    |
| `inset`    | A surface sunk into its host: a field, a track, a well             |
| `raised`   | A surface above the page: a button at rest, a chip, a pill         |
| `overlay`  | A surface the page floats over: a menu, a popover, a select's list |
| `modal`    | A surface the page waits for: a dialog, a sheet                    |
| `inverse`  | The reversed surface: a toast, a tooltip                           |
| `glass`    | A control over a photo                                             |
| `accent`   | The brand's own surface: a filled button, a switch that is on      |
| `knob`     | The thumb a control moves: a switch's knob, a slider's handle      |
| `hover`    | The pointer's treatment of the surface under it                    |
| `pressed`  | The press's treatment of the surface under it                      |
| `disabled` | A control that cannot act                                          |

Every finish states a `foreground` — the ink that sits on it — so a component needs no fallback, and `shadow` names the parts of the theme's scale (`["{shadow.edge.surface}", "{shadow.sm}"]`) instead of writing one: `elevation("md")` gives the same values on its own. A theme that paints flat leaves `gradient` out and gets `null`, so the component draws no background image.

The `material` says what the platform's own glass should be: `null` (every theme but the glassed ones, which state `"none"` and compile to `null`), or `apple` — `{ glass: "regular" | "clear", tint }` — which rides inside `finish.<role>` as `glassEffect` and `glassTintColor`, so a spread of the finish carries it. `ios`, `macos` and `windows` are props, not style keys, which `platformMaterial(role)` returns for the view that draws the finish:

```tsx
<View {...platformMaterial("overlay")} style={{ ...finish.overlay }} />
```

Both follow `selectTheme` and the appearance, and with `material: null` the view is drawn as before. The library's own popovers, hover cards, toasts, the editor's find bar and a glass carousel arrow spread it; the popups of `Menu`, `Select` and `Popover` on `nsh/base` take only `popupStyle`, so there the glass keys apply and the platform props do not.

The `apple` theme fills in `material.apple`: `glass`, `overlay` and `raised` carry `{ glass: "regular" }` (Liquid Glass on iOS and macOS 26+), and every other finish is a flat fill with a hairline edge. The `material` theme uses Material 3 Expressive tonal surfaces, circular corners, 8/10/10% state layers, press ripple (`state.ripple: true`), and `material.android.elevation` on elevated surfaces. The `winui` theme uses WinUI 3 (Windows 11) fill and stroke tokens, 4/8-point circular corners, Segoe UI Variable, Consolas, double focus rings, timing motion, underline tab and box-underline field indicators, and `material.windows` blur on `glass`, `overlay` and `inverse`. `nativeTheme()` from `theme-native` picks the theme of the platform the app runs on — Apple's on iOS and macOS, Material on Android, WinUI 3 on Windows, and the NSH Gallery theme everywhere else:

```npm
npx shadcn-nsh@latest init --theme native
```

```tsx
import { nativeTheme } from "./themes/native";

// Before mount: the first frame is already the platform's theme.
selectTheme(nativeTheme());
```

`init --theme apple` builds the app on Apple's palette; `--theme native` builds it on the NSH Gallery theme and installs both, for `nativeTheme()` to choose between at run time. On macOS 26+ an explicit `macos.backdrop` wins over `glassEffect`, so `apple` states none; it states `ios.backdrop` as the blur for iOS before 26.

Windows' Mica is not a finish: it is the window's own `backdrop` in `nsh-desktop` (Windows 11 maps it to Mica or Acrylic, macOS to a visual effect material), set once by the app in `nsh.json` and shown through surfaces whose fill is translucent:

```json
{ "window": { "backdrop": "window" } }
```

Spread one where a control needs that depth:

```tsx
<View style={{ backgroundColor: colors.raised, ...finish.raised, borderRadius: shape.control }} />
```

## Radii [#radii]

`theme.json`'s `cssVars.theme` block defines three corner radii, one per layer: `radius-control` (in-page elements: fields, rows, chips, badges, wells, colour areas, keycaps), `radius-container` (cards, menus, popovers, rich tooltips, list panels, toasts) and `radius-modal` (dialogs, sheets, drawers). shadcn's own `radius` slot equals `radius-control`. `shape` resolves each role reactively via `token()`, and `buttonCorner(size)` reads `controls().button.corner` (`"control"` or `"full"` capsule):

```tsx
import { buttonCorner, shape } from "@shadcn-nsh/theme";

shape.control; // 8, from radius-control
shape.container; // 12, from radius-container
shape.modal; // 14, from radius-modal
buttonCorner("default"); // 999 when button.corner.md is "full", else shape.control
```

| Theme               | `control` | `container` | `modal` | Buttons   |
| ------------------- | --------- | ----------- | ------- | --------- |
| `default`, `shadcn` | 8         | 12          | 14      | `control` |
| `solid-glass`       | 11        | 14          | 20      | `control` |
| `apple`             | 8         | 12          | 26      | capsule   |
| `material`          | 4         | 12          | 28      | capsule   |
| `winui`             | 4         | 8           | 8       | `control` |

A surface inside another takes a concentric corner from its outer one: `rounded(outer, inset)` gives `outer − inset`, never below 0. `rounded()` also puts the corner on with `shape.curve` (`"continuous"` or `"circular"`):

```tsx
import { rounded, shape } from "@shadcn-nsh/theme";

const card = { ...rounded(shape.container) };
const thumb = { ...rounded(shape.control, 2) }; // inside a 2-point track
```

## Reading the theme [#reading-the-theme]

```tsx
import { alpha, colors, finish, focusRing, rounded, shape } from "@shadcn-nsh/theme";

const card = {
  backgroundColor: colors.card,
  borderColor: colors.border,
  ...rounded(shape.container),
  boxShadow: finish.card.boxShadow,
};

const ring = focusRing(); // the keyboard focus outline
const dim = alpha(colors.foreground, 0.4); // a color at 40%
```

`focusRing(offset)` is the shared keyboard outline: the muted `ring` edge and a 3-point halo of `ring` at 30%. `hovered()` is the pointer's fill, the `hover` token (plus `stateLayer("hover")` when `state.overlay.hover > 0`). `alpha(color, a)` is a `color-mix` of that color with transparency. `colors`, `finish`, `shape` and `style()` are reactive: read them where they are used.

## Override from nsh.json [#override-from-nshjson]

An app's `nsh.json` sets the look in two places, and the two do not merge:

| Key in `nsh.json` | What it sets                                                                | When it is read                                                                 |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"theme"`         | the path to `theme.json`: every base token — colours, the `radius-*` tokens | on each read, at runtime — so `setTheme`, `setThemeOverrides`, `shape` reach it |
| `"tailwind"`      | the app's own class strings: `colors`, `fontFamily`, `spacing`, `radius`, … | when the app is built, into the class strings — no component here reads it      |

Components take their look from `"theme"`: `colors`, `finish`, `shape` and `font` read the tokens where they are used. `"tailwind"` shapes class names — which this library writes too (`bg-muted`, `text-sm`, `h-8`) — but it is fixed at build time, so nothing in it can follow `setTheme`. NSH's [theme tokens](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind#theme-tokens) has the rule in full.

**A colour named in `"tailwind"` wins over the token of the same name.** With `"colors": { "primary": "#3366ff" }`, every `bg-primary` in the app draws blue — pagination's selected page, a data table's move indicator — while `colors.primary` in JSX stays the theme's citrus. One name, two colours, and the panels drawn by class are the ones that differ. Set the role in `"theme"` instead.

The theme file stays complete: copy it, then edit. A shadcn slot it leaves out falls back to shadcn's neutral (see [Colors](#colors)), and `semantics.json` names tokens with `{token}`, so both appearances need the same set.

Add a colour the app's own classes use (both appearances — a token in one alone is not a token):

```json
{
  "cssVars": {
    "light": { "brand-alt": "oklch(0.65 0.14 300)" },
    "dark": { "brand-alt": "oklch(0.72 0.12 300)" }
  }
}
```

Change a role: `primary` in `cssVars.light` and `cssVars.dark`. Change a radius: `radius-control`, `radius-container` or `radius-modal` in `cssVars.theme` (keep `radius` equal to `radius-control`) — every corner follows them: `shape.*` and `rounded()` in the styles, and `rounded-(--radius…)` in the classes, this library's and the app's own alike. Fonts are the app's own: see [Fonts](#fonts).

## Fonts [#fonts]

A theme owns no font: none of the shipped themes declares a family, and one type scale (sizes and line heights) serves them all, so switching themes never reflows text. Each theme still states its own weight and letter spacing per role. Text names no family of its own; it takes the app's `font-sans`, and monospaced text (the `font-mono` class, code in a `Text`) takes `font-mono` — this library writes the generic `monospace` where it needs a monospaced face. Each of the 7 typography composites carries `fontFamily: "system-ui"` because DTCG requires the field, but the library never reads it. The user's system font size scales every size.

Set the app's families in the `cssVars.theme` block of its own `theme.json`:

```json
{
  "cssVars": {
    "theme": { "font-sans": "Inter, sans-serif", "font-mono": "JetBrains Mono, monospace" }
  }
}
```

NSH takes the first family of the list that is not a generic one (`system-ui`, `sans-serif`, `monospace` …), and a list of generics alone is the system's own font. That is why this library writes `monospace`: the system's monospaced font, not a font called "monospace".

A font file is the app's. Import it in TSX — the import registers it before the first frame, and its value is the family name the file declares, not the file name — and name that family in the theme:

```tsx
// app.tsx: the import bundles and registers the family; the app's `theme.json` names it.
import "./fonts/JetBrainsMono-Regular.ttf";
```

The side-effect import is deliberate: TypeScript drops an import whose value is unused, and the font with it, when the theme names the family as a string. A weight or an italic is a file of its own, `registerFont(bytes)` reads one the app did not ship, and the fallback after the app's family is what NSH draws for a family it cannot find — see NSH's [fonts](https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts#shipping-a-font).

This library distributes no font files: `add theme` writes JSON and TypeScript and names no family.

## Restyling [#restyling]

Edit the sources; every component follows. Change a brand color in `cssVars.light` and `cssVars.dark`, a radius in `cssVars.theme`, a shadow part in the DTCG `shadow` group, a gradient, style group or material in the theme's `tokens/` files. Keep the keys: components and finishes refer to them by name, and both appearances need the same merged finish shape — a finish you add states every field of its neighbours, and a value that follows the device is stated twice, `pointer` and `touch`, with the same keys — a theme that has its own device sizes writes them in `tokens/themes/<id>/pointer.tokens.json` and `touch.tokens.json`, and one that does not inherits the base set's.

- Add the theme to an app with `shadcn-nsh add theme` (or let `init` do it); subsequent `add` runs key-merge missing entries into `theme.json` and `semantics.json` while keeping your values.
- Replacing both files together rebrands the whole library; a key added upstream should be added here too.
- The demos on this site can draw in an installed theme: the **Demo theme** switch in the nav (Default, shadcn, Solid Glass, Apple, Material or WinUI 3) writes the demo app's palette and loads the panels again. The list is `apps/website/demos/palettes.ts`; a demo reads the palette before it mounts, so its first frame is already the chosen theme. Every palette — its install command and every role it sets — has a page linked from [Themes](./themes).
- To change one component's look instead, edit its look function in the copied component; to change structure or API, edit the shell. See [Customizing](./customizing).
- Maintaining this repository: edit the look in `packages/ui` (all of it is ours; a credit line in the header says where it began); `port:check` lists upstream's changes and `bun run port:review` marks them read. After editing `packages/theme`, run `bun run registry:build` and commit `public/r`.

Theme rules and decisions: [`docs/specs/design-semantics.md`](https://github.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/blob/main/docs/specs/design-semantics.md), [`docs/specs/theme-roles.md`](https://github.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/blob/main/docs/specs/theme-roles.md) and [`packages/theme/README.md`](https://github.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/blob/main/packages/theme/README.md). Behavior and accessibility are `nsh/base`'s: [nsh.dev/elements](https://nsh.dev/elements).

# Themes (/dev/docs/themes)

## One look, more than one palette [#one-look-more-than-one-palette]

A theme is one `AppTheme`: `theme.json` (base tokens: colours, three `radius-*` layer lengths, and fonts),
`semantics.json` (cross-platform semantics: style groups and `shared` + sparse `light` / `dark`
finishes, referencing tokens with `{token}`) and the `index.ts` that names it. An app is _built_
with one theme and can _carry_ more, switching between them while it runs with `selectTheme`.

Every demo on this site can be drawn in any of these palettes: pick one with the **Demo theme**
switch in the nav, and the previews load again in it. The panel above is the showcase — buttons, a
card with a field, badges, switches, a slider and a progress bar, with the card, inset and press finishes
the palette brings. The list is `apps/website/demos/palettes.ts`. Each palette has its own page,
with the same sections: how to install it, every token it sets, and every finish it draws. Those
pages read each theme's `theme.json` and `semantics.json`, following the
[design-semantics standard](https://github.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/blob/main/docs/specs/design-semantics.md)
and the [theme roles spec](https://github.com/aningdev/shadcn-nsh/blob/main/docs/specs/theme-roles.md).

## Radii by role [#radii-by-role]

`theme.json` states one corner radius per layer in `cssVars.theme` — `radius-control` (in-page
elements), `radius-container` (cards, menus, popovers, toasts) and `radius-modal` (dialogs, sheets) —
and `controls().button.corner.*` makes buttons capsules (`material`, touch `apple`) or points / `control` (the rest). A surface nested in
another takes the concentric corner, `rounded(outer, inset)`. Every corner that reads a theme radius
uses `shape.curve` (`"continuous"` or `"circular"`), which `rounded()` applies in one place.

<ThemeIndex />
